en: The Blessed Lord said: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat.
Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Śrīdhara:
In order to manifest His own appearance and disappearance,
Hari Himself praises Karma-yoga for the purpose of discerning the meaning of the terms "That" (Tat) and "Thou" (Tvam).
Thus, with these two chapters, the yoga of knowledge— which serves as the means for the yoga of action— has been declared as a means to liberation.

Now, intending to elaborate upon that very same [knowledge] by prescribing qualities such as "offering to Brahman" and so forth, and by means of the discrimination between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, the Blessed One first spoke with three verses beginning with "This," praising it because it has not been attained elsewhere.
It is called "imperishable" because its fruit is imperishable.
In ancient times, I taught this yoga to Vivasvat, the son of Aditi; and he, in turn, taught it to his son Manu, the god of ancestral rites.
And that Manu spoke it to his own son, Ikṣvāku. //1//
Madhusūdana:

Although previously two yogas were taught— namely, the yoga of knowledge as the goal (*upeya*) and the yoga of action as the means (*upāya*)— nevertheless, by the statement, "He who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees" (Gītā 5.6), [the Lord now teaches their non-difference].

Metaphorically attributing unity to the goal and the means because their fruit is one, the Blessed One praises the path of action (*karma-yoga*), which serves as the means, and the path of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), which is the goal, by recounting the lineage in order to prescribe various virtues.
He [taught] this yoga— characterized by steadfastness in knowledge and attainable through the means of steadfastness in action— to Vivasvat, as described in these two chapters.

I, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the protector of the entire world, spoke— meaning I spoke thoroughly, in the form of cutting away all doubts and so forth— to Āditya, who is the seed of the lineage of all Kṣatriyas, at the time of creation and other such occasions, in order to protect the entire world by strengthening the kings upon whom it depends.

He shows by way of distinction how strength is gained through this: "Imperishable" (*avyaya*) means that because its root is the imperishable Veda and because its fruit is imperishable, it does not fall away from its own fruit; thus it is "imperishable," meaning its fruit is unfailing.
The sense is that strengthening is possible by means of such [knowledge].
And he, my disciple Vivasvat, spoke it to Manu Vaivasvata, his own son.
And that Manu spoke it to his own son Ikṣvāku, the first king;

although this instruction concerning the Lord is common to all Manvantaras beginning with Svāyambhuva, nevertheless, with reference to the present Vaivasvata Manvantara, the lineage of the tradition is calculated starting from Āditya. //1//
Viśvanātha: In the fourth [chapter], for the sake of manifesting his own nature, he states the eternality of his birth and activities,
as well as the expansion of his own teachings on the excellence of knowledge arising from the sacrifice to Brahman and so forth.
With these two chapters, he praises the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga), which is to be accomplished through action free from desire (niṣkāma-karma), beginning with the words "this" (imam). //1//
Baladeva:
In the fourth [chapter], he establishes the cause of his own manifestation, the eternality of his own pastimes, and the yoga of knowledge within virtuous actions.
This very Lord, the delighter of Devakī, has also proclaimed the supreme majesty of knowledge.

Having unified the path of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) and the path of action (*karma-yoga*) taught in the two preceding chapters because they share a single fruit, He praises their lineage by saying "this":
"I have declared this to you, O Sūrya.
It is "imperishable" (*avyaya*) because it is eternal, as it is not subject to decay, and because its fruit does not deviate from its own result.
And that disciple of mine, Vivasvat, declared it to his son Manu Vaivasvata;
and that Manu spoke it to his own son Ikṣvāku. //1//
Thus, this [yoga] was received through a succession of teachers; the royal sages knew it.
Over a long period of time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga has been lost here on earth. (4.2)
Śrīdhara: "Thus" means "in this way"; that is, those kings and those sages. Others as well, such as Nimi and other royal sages (rājarṣis), are also included.
Their ancestors, headed by Ikṣvāku, knew and understood this exalted yoga.
He states the reason for its being unknown to those of the present day: "O scorcher of foes, that yoga has perished and been lost from this world due to the power of time. (2)
Madhusūdana:

Thus, this Yoga, which has been received through the lineage of teacher and disciple beginning with Āditya, is known by the royal sages (*rājarṣis*)— namely, those kings and sages such as Nimi and others who, possessing sovereign power, are capable of discerning subtle matters, and who have learned it as taught by their own fathers and ancestors.

Therefore, because it is rooted in the beginningless Veda, possesses infinite fruit, and has been transmitted through an unbroken succession of teachers and disciples from time immemorial, this Yoga is free from any suspicion of being artificial; thus it is praised for the sake of generating extraordinary faith as a practice of great power. Although this Yoga is so highly purposeful, due to the long passage of time which causes the decline of Dharma, it has now [reached such a state].

"At the time of our own dispensation, at the end of the Dvāpara age, having encountered those who were weak, of uncontrolled senses, and lacking qualification, [the Vedic path] was overcome by lust, anger, and other passions; it became lost and its traditional transmission was severed.
Alas, what a misfortune for the world that, without it, the goals of human life cannot be attained!"—thus the Blessed Lord laments.

O scorcher of foes (*parantapa*): he is called a "scorcher of foes" because, like the sun, he scorches with his powerful heroism, discernment, and austerity the enemy host consisting of desire, anger, and so forth; the meaning is that he is a scorcher of enemies who has conquered his senses, as evidenced by his wondrous deeds such as the disregard for Urvaśī.
Therefore, it indicates that you are qualified for this because you have conquered your senses. //2//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Thus, the royal sages (rājarṣis) knew this yoga—which had been received through the lineage of teacher and disciple beginning with Vivasvat—as having been taught by their own fathers and others, such as Ikṣvāku; [yet] in this world, it was lost, its tradition having been interrupted. //2//
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today, because you are My devotee and My friend; for this is indeed the supreme secret. (4.3)
Śrīdhara: "This very same [Yoga]—
this very Yoga which was once interrupted in its tradition— is now spoken by Me to you again,
because you are My devotee and My friend."
It is not told by me to anyone else, for this is the supreme secret. //3//
Madhusūdana:
Although this [knowledge] was thus previously taught, it became one whose lineage of transmission was interrupted due to the absence of qualified recipients;
and without it, the goal of human life is not attained.

This very same yoga, which is ancient and has come down through a beginningless succession of teachers, has been taught by me today—out of great affection for you—to you alone at this time when the tradition is on the verge of interruption; it has not been told to anyone else. Why? Because you are my devotee and my friend.
The word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetau*).

Since you are my devotee, and while being one who has come for refuge, you are exceedingly affectionate, a friend of equal age, and a tender companion who remains so at all times—for this reason [the teaching] has been told to you; such is the meaning.
To the question, "Why is it not told to another?", he says:
For indeed, this knowledge is supreme, a secret, and most strictly to be guarded. //3//
Viśvanātha: The reason why this was spoken specifically to you is twofold: [the states of being] a devotee, a servant, and a friend.
But others hold that the reasons for its being "inexpressible" apply only to those who are modern [or of limited vision]. //3//

Baladeva said: "That very yoga, which is expressed by those words in their proper sequence, has been declared by me to you—my friend, who is exceedingly dear to me and my companion—because you are my devotee, have sought refuge in me, and are my friend; it has not been told to anyone else."
In this context, the reason is "it is a secret"; for [the word] "hi" means "because," since this is the supreme secret and is therefore to be concealed. //3//
Arjuna said:
Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier.
How may I understand this, that you spoke it at the beginning? //4//

Śrīdhara: Seeing the impossibility of the Lord’s instruction in yoga to Vivasvat, Arjuna said, "The later," etc. Your birth is later, i.e., more recent; the birth of Vivasvat is earlier, i.e., belonging to a prior time.
Therefore, because you are of recent origin, how could I know—that is, how could I be able to understand—this fact that you first taught the yoga to Vivasvat, who is of ancient lineage? //4//
Madhusūdana:

Arjuna, repeating that doubt which fools have regarding the Blessed Vāsudeva—namely, the suspicion that He is not omniscient and not eternal because of His human nature—raises the following objection: "The other [birth]...
This means the birth in the house of Vasudeva, which occurred at the present time and is of recent duration, as well as the assumption of a body, which is inferior due to being human.
However, the birth of Vivasvat was long ago, occurring at the beginning of creation and being preeminent due to his divine status;
since the absence of the Self's birth has already been established previously, Arjuna’s question refers exclusively to the birth of the body.
Therefore, how may I understand this so that its meaning is not contradictory? He explains the very meaning of these words:
"In the beginning, you taught Yoga."

The sense is that this is a contradictory statement: that you, a human being of the present time who are not omniscient, have spoken to the omniscient Āditya of a former age at the beginning of creation.
Here is the distilled meaning:
does this [alleged] teaching of yours to Āditya occur through you as unconditioned by this body, conditioned by another body, or by means of this very body?
Not the first, because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to remember what was experienced in another birth;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that I too would remember what was experienced in another birth.

Because there is no distinction between you and me in being human and thus lacking omniscience; as it has been said by the learned: "And that which was experienced in another birth is not remembered. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because at the beginning of creation, the present body does not yet exist.

Thus, since existence at the beginning of creation is impossible for one with another body, there are two prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣas) against Arjuna's position: namely, that [the Self] is not omniscient and is not eternal. //4//
Viśvanātha:
He asks about another [matter] pertaining to the present time, because the matter already stated is impossible; the implication is: "Since the former is ancient, how am I to believe this? //4//

Baladeva: To refute those ignorant ones who harbor doubts regarding Kṛṣṇa’s eternality and omniscience, Arjuna said, "The later" (*aparam*). How may I understand—that is, how may I believe—this: that you, who are recent (*ādhunika*), spoke this yoga to Vivasvat, who is ancient (*prācīna*)?
This is the meaning.

Indeed, Arjuna does not fail to know Kṛṣṇa as the Lord of All, for He possesses that very nature by virtue of being His incarnation known as a man; moreover, this is confirmed by Kṛṣṇa’s own words such as "the supreme abode, the supreme abode.
However, he asks "another" and so forth not because of a doubt regarding His omniscience, but rather to dispel the suspicion of those who are ignorant.
Just as that Lord of All knows His own true nature, no one else does;
therefore, for the welfare of the world, His form, birth, and other attributes must be revealed from His lotus-like mouth alone.
To that end, He should not be accused of boasting when He proclaims His own majesty.
However, it is indeed worthy of praise due to its compassion.

And this question—concerning the nature, birth, and so forth of You, the Supreme Brahman in human form, which are extraordinary compared to the world, as to what they are like, for what purpose, and at what time—is posed like a command even to one who knows; its purpose is to provide an answer that dispels the doubts of the ignorant. //4//
The Blessed Lord said: Many births of Mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna.
I know all of them, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
Śrīdhara: With the intention that [the Lord] has taught by means of another form, the Blessed Lord spoke the reply beginning with "Many...
He says, "I know them"—that is, I know them—because His power of knowledge is never lost.
But you neither know nor do you understand, because you are enveloped by ignorance. //5//
Madhusūdana:
Regarding that, he provides the solution for the first [objection] by means of His omniscience with the words "Many...

(bahunīti). Births—meaning the assumption of bodies for divine play (*līlā*)—have passed away for Me, who am like the rising of the sun, according to the perspective of worldly perception; whereas for you, who are ignorant, they are merely the assumption of bodies acquired through karma.

The phrase "and yours" is an elliptical expression intended to include all other living beings as well, or else it is spoken with the intention of emphasizing the oneness of the individual soul (jīva).
O Arjuna!
Addressing him by the name of the Arjuna tree, the Lord indicates that his knowledge is obscured.
"I—the omniscient, omnipotent Lord—know all those births: my own, yours, and those of others.
But you, an ignorant individual soul whose power of knowledge is veiled, do not know even your own; how much less can you know those belonging to others?"
O scorcher of foes (*parantapa*):

by addressing you thus, he indicates that you are deluded because you have displayed a perverted vision, having set out to kill another who is merely imagined as an enemy through a dualistic perspective.
Thus, by these two forms of address, both obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*) are shown to be qualities of ignorance (*ajñāna*). //5//
Viśvanātha says: With the intention of explaining that [the Lord] taught through another incarnation, he says "many" (*bahūni*).

Regarding the words "and of you" (*tava ca*), the meaning is that whenever there was an incarnation of mine, at that very time your manifestation also occurred, because you were my attendant (*pārṣada*).
"I know"—I know because of my omniscience as the Lord of all.
"You do not know" means that I have obscured your knowledge for the sake of accomplishing my own pastimes; such is the sense.
Therefore, O scorcher of foes!
By the mere pride of being the son of Kuntī at present, you cause your enemies to suffer. //5//

Baladeva: With the intention that the Lord, assuming within Himself many eternally established forms—as declared in such scriptural passages as "I am indeed one; though being one, I appear as many"—taught Him [the truth] previously through another form, he says, "The Lord [assumed] many [forms]."
"And yours" means that because you were my friend, you too had as many births; the sense is:
"But you do not know this," because at present, for the sake of accomplishing My own pastimes through inconceivable power, I have concealed your knowledge.

By this, his own omniscience is demonstrated. Here, the reality of the births of the Blessed One is to be understood from the statement "many," etc., spoken from the mouth of Śrī, and from the example "of you" as well.
Nor is there the modification called birth, because that has been refuted by the subsequent explanation. //5//
Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own divine power (māyā).
Śrīdhara: But how can there be birth for you who are beginningless?
And how can there be birth again for one who is indestructible, such that it is said, "many births have passed for me"?
Furthermore, how can there be birth for you, the Lord, who are devoid of merit and demerit, in the same manner as that of an individual soul (jīva)?
Therefore he says, "Even though unborn.
This is true;
nevertheless, even though I am unborn—that is, devoid of birth—[I appear].
Likewise, although I am of an imperishable nature and eternal,
and although I am the Lord and free from dependence on karma,
I manifest through my own *māyā*; that is, I come into being precisely through the power of my unimpaired knowledge, strength, valor, and other faculties.
[Objection: "But even so, how can there be birth for you, who are devoid of a physical body composed of the sixteen constituents (kalās)?
[Response: Therefore it is said: 'Having presided over—meaning having assumed—my own nature consisting of pure sattva.
The meaning is: 'I descend by my own will in a form of perfectly pure and powerful sattva. //6//
Madhusūdana:

If you indeed remember the possession of many past births by the self, then you are a *jāti-smara* (one who remembers former births); for even the knowledge of another's birth belongs to a yogin through the conceit of universal identity (*sārvātmyābhimāna*), whereas instruction is given through the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstra-dṛṣṭi*), as in the case of Vāmadeva (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.30).
This is possible according to reason.
Thus Vāmadeva said in the *Dāśatayī*: "I, though a living soul (*jīva*), was Manu; I was Sūrya; I am the seer Kakṣīvān, the sage," and so forth.
Therefore, you are not an omniscient being in the primary sense.
And thus, being himself non-Īśvara, how could he have taught Āditya as omniscient?
For primary omniscience is not possible for a *jīva*, because the individual limiting adjunct (*vyaṣṭy-upādhi*) is limited and lacks connection with all things.

Furthermore, even for the *virāj*—the collective limiting adjunct (*samaṣṭy-upādhi*)—knowledge regarding the objects that are transformations of subtle elements and transformations of *māyā* is impossible, since its limiting adjunct consists of gross elements.

Thus, it is established that even for Hiraṇyagarbha, who possesses a subtle material substrate (*sūkṣma-bhūtopādhi*), there is an absence of knowledge regarding the sequence of creation— such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth— which is the transformation of *māyā*, the cause of that [substrate].
Therefore, the Lord (*īśvara*) alone, because he possesses a causal substrate, is the primary omniscient one, possessing knowledge whose objects comprise all things— past, future, and present.

Whether there are three illusory functions (*māyā-vṛtti*) with respect to past, future, and present objects, or whether there is a single illusory function encompassing all objects—this is another point. Furthermore, for that eternal and omniscient Lord, birth is logically impossible due to the absence of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth; indeed, the state of possessing numerous past births is utterly discarded. Thus, while addressing the two doubts—that if he were a *jīva* (individual soul), omniscience would be impossible, and if he were the Lord (*īśvara*), the assumption of a body would be impossible—he states the following to refute even the position of his being non-eternal: "Unborn" (*aja*).
"Joy!
Birth is the grasping of a new body, sense-faculties, and so forth;
passing away is the separation from the previously grasped body, sense-faculties, and so forth."
That which is called "non-existence after death" by the logicians has been stated [by the Blessed One]: "For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain" (Gītā 2.27).
And both of these occur through the power of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
The state of being subject to merit and demerit belongs to the ignorant *jīva* who identifies with the body, because such a one possesses the qualification for ritual action (*karma*).
In this regard, what is said—that it is not possible for the omniscient Lord, the cause of all, to assume such a body—is indeed correct.
Why? If His body were an effect of the gross elements, then, in its individual form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), He would exist in the waking state and be equal to ourselves and others.
And when it is in its collective form (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*), it possesses the nature of the Virāj-jīva because that is its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Alternatively, when it is the effect of the subtle elements (*sūkṣma-bhūta-kārya*), then in its individual form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), it is in the state of dreaming and is similar to ourselves and others;
and in its collective form, it possesses the nature of the Hiraṇyagarbha-jīva because that is its limiting adjunct.
And thus it is established that it is simply impossible for the Supreme Lord to enter a material body inhabited by a *jīva*.
Nor should it be argued that His entry into such a body inhabited by a *jīva* is like the possession of a living being (*bhūtāveśa*).

If it were accepted that the experience of that living soul occurs through the limitation of that specific body, then since the Lord’s entry into all bodies exists by way of His form as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), the acceptance of a specific body would be redundant;
and if there were no experience, it would be logically untenable for it to be the body of a living soul.
Therefore, with the first half-verse, He accepts that the Lord does not possess a material body: "Though being unborn and of imperishable nature, though being the Lord of beings..."

By the words "though being unborn" (ajo 'pi san), He negates the assumption of a new body; by "though being the imperishable Self" (avyayātmāpi san), He negates the severance of the previous body; and by "though being the Lord of all beings"—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—He negates the state of being subject to merit and demerit, which characterizes those who possess the qualities of the Blessed One. If so, how then does He assume a body? He explains this with the second half of the verse: "Presiding over My own nature, I come into being."

Presiding over my own *prakṛti*, known as *māyā*—which possesses manifold diverse powers, is exceedingly skillful at effecting the impossible, and serves as my own material cause—I bring it under control through the reflection of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*) and manifest myself by means of its specific transformations alone, thereby accomplishing the state of being the cause of the universe. Operating solely through my own will, my form consists of pure *sattva*; such is the nature of that which is qualified by it.
Thus, his state of being unborn, undecaying, and sovereign is established.
Therefore, it is logical that with this very eternal body, I taught this yoga to Vivasvat and to you.
And so says the Śruti: "Brahman has space as its body. Space...
It is not indeterminate (avyākṛta),
because it is seen as such in passages such as, "That is woven both lengthwise and crosswise in space alone" (BAU 3.8.7),
and because of the logical principle: "Space [is the cause], on account of its characteristic marks" (VS 1.1.22).
If it is asked, "In that case, since there is no material body, how is there the perception of human nature and so forth in Him?", he says in response: "by My own *māyā*.

The meaning is that the perception of human nature and so forth in Me occurs solely through My *māyā* for the sake of favoring the world, and not according to the actual state of reality (*vastu-vṛtti*).
Thus it has been said in the *Mokṣadharma*:
"O Nārada, this which you see me as is indeed an illusion created by me;
you ought not to see me as endowed with the qualities of all beings.
The meaning is: "You ought not to see me—with my physical eyes—as possessed of the qualities of all beings, that is, as having the causal adjuncts (upādhi)."

And it has been said by the venerable commentator: "That Blessed One, ever endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor, having brought under his control His own Māyā— Prakṛti, which consists of the three guṇas and belongs to Viṣṇu— though unborn, undecaying, the Lord of beings, and by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, yet through His own Māyā appears as if possessing a body and as if born."
And he is observed to perform favor for the world even in the absence of any personal motive, out of a desire to show compassion toward living beings.
Furthermore, the commentators have stated that he came into being with a divine form fashioned by his own will, consisting of *māyā*.
That which is eternal is the causal adjunct (*upādhi*) called *māyā*, which possesses manifold powers.
That very [body] is the body of the Blessed One; such is the opinion of the authors of the Bhāṣya.
Others, however, do not accept the relationship of body and embodied being (*deha-dehibhāva*) in the case of the Supreme Lord.

They maintain that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— who is eternal, all-pervading, a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*), perfect, devoid of material qualities (*nirguṇa*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)— is Himself that very form, and not some other form composed of elements or consisting of *māyā*.

In this view, the interpretation is as follows: "And like space, it is all-pervading and eternal," because of such scriptural texts as, "Verily, this Self is indestructible, for its nature is not subject to destruction" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14);
and because of the principle, "But non-existence is impossible, since what exists cannot cease to be" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.3.8).

According to the reasoning beginning with "Not the Self, because of the absence of scriptural statement and because of its eternity" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.16), and by the very nature of reality, although I am devoid of birth and destruction,
the illuminator of all, and the Lord of all beings as the substratum of the Māyā that is the cause of all, I [assume] *prakṛti*,
which is my own nature (*svabhāva*), consisting of the single essence of the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
"He turns away his own māyā" means his own essential nature (*nija-svarūpa*);
for the Śruti says: "O Blessed One, in what is he established? In his own greatness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Abiding in my own essential nature (*sva-svarūpa*), remaining established in that very nature, I manifest; though devoid of the relationship between body and embodied, I act as if possessing a body.

If it is asked, "How can there be a perception of corporeality in that which is bodiless—a dense mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-ghana*)?", he says: "by means of my own *māyā*.

The meaning is this: the perception of me, the Lord Vāsudeva—who am without qualities (*nirguṇa*), pure, a dense mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and devoid of the relationship between body and embodied—as having such a form is merely *māyā*. As it has been said:
"Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves; for the welfare of the world, He appears here through His illusory power as if possessing a body. Thus [it is said].
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for the cowherds of Nanda and the inhabitants of Vraja!
And as it is said: "The eternal Brahman is the supreme bliss, the full.

However, some maintain that even though the supreme bliss is eternal, partless, and changeless, its possession of parts and its manifestation are indeed real; we do not refute those who speak thus without logical justification, according to the maxim: "One should not find fault with those who speak without reason."
If it were possible [to establish this], let it be so; why further prolixity? Thus, we desist. //5//
Viśvanātha:
He describes the manner of His own birth: "Though unborn"—that is, though being devoid of birth—"I manifest," appearing among gods, humans, animals, and so forth.
Is this not a wonder?

Even the individual soul (*jīva*), though in reality unborn, is indeed born after the destruction of the gross body. To this, he replies: "He whose body is the imperishable Self, which is indestructible."
Furthermore, for the individual soul (jīva), there is indeed non-origination (ajatva) by its own essential nature which is distinct from its body;
its possession of birth exists only through its connection with a body produced by ignorance (avidyā).
For me, however, because of my status as the Lord (īśvara), both non-origination—as being non-different from my own body—and the possession of birth are established by my very nature.
And that [birth] is indeed wonderful and inconceivable because it is difficult to reconcile;

therefore, he says—meaning "even though I am the Lord of beings"—that there is no fear of birth for me in good or evil wombs like that of a living soul (*jīva*) possessed of merit, demerit, and so forth, since I am free from dependence on karma.
Now, it may be objected: a *jīva* indeed attains bodies such as those of gods, which are reached through karma, by means of its own bondage, the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*).

You are the Supreme Lord, devoid of a physical mark (liṅga), all-pervading, and the controller of karma, time, and so forth; indeed, according to the Vedic revelation "May I become many," You manifest in the form of the entire universe.
Furthermore, that You specifically say, "Even though I am such as this, I come into being," [is significant].
Therefore, I consider that Your birth is understood as being for the purpose of manifesting in the world certain eternal, specific bodies that are distinct from all other beings in the universe.
To the question "How indeed is that so?", He says: "presiding over My own nature" (*prakṛtiṃ svām adhiṣṭhāya*).
Here, if by the word *prakṛti* the external power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) is meant, [then...]
In that case, since the Supreme Lord, as its presiding authority, indeed becomes the form of the universe through that [power], no distinction is perceived.
Therefore, because these two—*saṃsiddhi* and *prakṛti*—are designated as "own-form" (*svarūpa*) and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), the word *prakṛti* here refers only to the own-form;
it does not refer to the power of *māyā*, which constitutes that own-form.
And its essential nature is indeed existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*).
"For this very reason, You are Nature whose essence is pure being (*śuddha-sattva*)," so said the venerable Svāmī-carana.

"Having taken recourse to my own *prakṛti*, which is my very nature (*svabhāva*), I manifest by means of my own form through my own will"—this is the meaning, according to the venerable Śrī Rāmānujācārya.

He explains that "my own *prakṛti*, which is my nature," refers to that which has the singular essence of the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-ghanaika-rasa*); he excludes *māyā* [from this], meaning it is his own essential nature (*nija-svarūpa*).

"He, O Blessed One, in what is He established? "In His own majesty," according to the Śruti. "Abiding in my own essential nature, I manifest while remaining established in that very nature; I conduct myself as if possessing a body, even though devoid of the distinction between body and embodied self," so said the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī. Now, if you are indeed the immutable Self, whose very nature is the imperishable Fish, Tortoise, and so forth, [how can there be such manifestation?]
In that case, why are your manifest form and your previously manifest forms not perceived simultaneously?

To this he replies: "By that Māyā which has become my very self"—meaning by that *yoga-māyā*, which is a function of the power of consciousness (*cic-śakti*), whose activity consists of both concealing one's own true nature and revealing it. For by that [Māyā], having first concealed the forms descended in previous times and revealed the present form, I come into being.
"I exist by means of my own *māyā*—that is, precisely through the power of unimpaired knowledge, strength, valor, and so forth," says the venerable Svāmicaraṇa.
Here, the word *māyā* is a synonym for knowledge, as in the phrase "knowledge (*māyā*) is wisdom (*vayuna*)," meaning self-knowledge.
Thus, there is the usage of the learned: "By *māyā* he constantly knows the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of the ancients," says the venerable Śrī Rāmānujācāryacaraṇa.

"In me, the Blessed One Vāsudeva, who am devoid of the relation of body and embodied, the perception [of me] in that form is mere illusion (māyāmātra)," so said the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī. //6//
Baladeva: By describing His own nature and birth as being distinct from the world, He declares His own eternity with the words "Though unborn" (ajo 'pi).

Here, the word *prakṛti* is a synonym for essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherent disposition (*svabhāva*). "Presiding over my own nature" (*svāṃ prakṛtim*) means taking recourse to or relying upon my own essential nature; "I manifest" (*sambhavāmi*) means I appear.
These two, however, are synonyms for *saṃsiddhi* (accomplishment): "own-form" (*svarūpa*) and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), according to Amara;
thus, [the meaning is] "I manifest by my very own-form."
He specifies this point in order to investigate its meaning with the words "even though unborn," and so forth.
The word *api* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
Birth (*janma*) is the connection with a body not previously possessed.
Being indeed devoid of that [intellect],
and being one whose self (ātman)— meaning whose intellect and so forth— is imperishable (avyaya), i.e., free from transformation; for it is stated in such passages as "ātman means 'in a male'."
The meaning is: "even though being the Lord of all beings," that is, even while remaining the controller of other individual souls (*jīvas*).

The phrase "I descend by means of that very form which possesses qualities such as being unborn, and which is an omnipresent mass of knowledge and bliss" is an explanation of "I manifest myself in my own essential nature. It is clarified that for such a nature, birth is merely a manifestation—like that of the sun—and thus its distinctness from worldly phenomena and its eternal character are made evident.
The dependence on karma has been refuted.
And the Śruti says thus: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways.
And the Smṛti and direct perception also state: "The birth of Hari is in no way a modification," and so forth.
Therefore, it is recorded in the tradition that He was seen in the maternity chamber, possessing a divine form adorned with celestial weapons and endowed with the six opulences.
He states the purpose [of His appearance] as "by His own māyā";
the meaning is that it was for the sake of uplifting those living beings who worship Him, motivated by compassion for them.
"Māyā" [is used] in the senses of "deceit" and "compassion," according to the Viśva [Kośa].
Some [maintain it means] "by His own māyā," that is, by His own omniscience or His own volition;
for the Nirghaṇṭu lexicon states: "Māyā is wisdom (vayuna) and knowledge (jñāna)."

Indeed, worldly beings such as kings, abandoning their previous bodies and assuming new ones, become ignorant mortals devoid of continuity; the distinctiveness of Hari from such a mortal is manifest. By the phrase "though he is the Lord of all beings," even those such as yogis who have attained supernatural powers are excluded.

Hari is a mass of blissful consciousness; although He is devoid of distinction between body and embodied soul, or between quality and the possessor of qualities, through the power of His own particularity, He is perceived by the wise in various forms. //6//
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata, and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself. (4.7)
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry "When do you arise?", he says, "Whenever...
*Glāniḥ* means loss;
*abhyutthānam* means increase. //7//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, as to how and for what purpose You, who are a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*), engage in worldly activity like an embodied being—that is explained by the words "whenever" (*yadā yadā*).

[This refers to] *dharma*, which is enjoined by the Vedas, which is the means for the prosperity and liberation (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*) of living beings, and is characterized by engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*).

Whenever there is decline or decay of the *varṇas* and *āśramas*, and of the conduct manifested by them— O Bhārata (the meaning of the address being that, because you are born in the lineage of Bharata,
or because you delight in *bhā*, which is knowledge, you are not able to endure the loss of Dharma)—
whenever there is likewise the emergence or rise of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is forbidden by the Vedas and is the cause of manifold sufferings.
Then, for those who oppose the Dharma, I create a body as My own self; though eternally established, I manifest it as if newly created through Māyā. //7//
Viśvanātha:
In response to the expectation of when he would be born, he says, "When...
The sense is that, being unable to endure those two—the decline (glāni) or loss of dharma and the rise (abhyutthāna) or increase of adharma—he intended to bring about their reversal.
"I create myself as the body; though eternally perfected, I manifest that which is already created through my illusory power (māyā)," so says the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī. //7//
Baladeva: Now he states the time of his manifestation with the words "When...

When there is the decline—that is, the destruction—of Dharma as declared in the Vedas, and the rise—that is, the emergence—of Adharma which is its opposite, then I manifest myself; I do not create myself anew because I am eternally established. Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the time of my manifestation. //7//
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked, and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age. (4.8)
Śrīdhara: To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "For the protection" (paritrāṇāya);
that is, for the protection of the virtuous who abide in their own duty (svadharma).
They are called "evil-doers" because they perform wicked deeds; and for their destruction—
thus, for the purpose of establishing the Dharma, one should stabilize the Dharma by protecting the virtuous and slaying the wicked.
The meaning is that I manifest at each respective juncture and on each such occasion.
Furthermore, one should not suspect cruelty on the part of one who thus effects the suppression of the wicked;
as it has been said: "Just as there is no lack of compassion in a mother toward her child, whether she is fondling it or striking it."
That very [state] belongs to Maheśa, the controller of both merit and demerit. //8//
Madhusūdana:

Is it then that the decline of dharma and the increase of adharma are the cause of your satisfaction, such that you manifest at that very time? In that case, your incarnation would indeed bring about misfortune. To this he says "for the protection" (paritrāṇāya) and so forth. [He replies: No.

For the protection—that is, for the preservation on all sides and in every way—of the virtuous who perform meritorious deeds and abide by the path of the Vedas as they decline through the loss of Dharma;

and likewise for the destruction of the evildoers who commit sins and oppose the path of the Vedas as they increase through the growth of Adharma; he explains how both of these may be accomplished: "for the sake of establishing Dharma," meaning by the complete warding off of Adharma.
For the sake of establishing [the world], for the protection of the Vedic path, and for the re-establishment of Dharma, I manifest as before in every age, age after age. //8//
Viśvanātha:
But surely even royal sages or Brahmin sages who are Your devotees are capable of warding off the decline of dharma and the increase of adharma; for what purpose, then, is this incarnation of Yours?
If this is so, it is true; however,
He says "pari" (even) to indicate that He is capable of performing other difficult deeds as well— namely,
the suffering in the form of distraction experienced by the virtuous who are His exclusive devotees and whose hearts are blossoming with longing for His vision.
Therefore, for their protection;
likewise, for the destruction of evildoers—such as Rāvaṇa, Kaṃsa, Keśin, and others—who cause suffering to My devotees and the world and cannot be slain by anyone other than Me;

and likewise, for the purpose of establishing the Dharma, so that the supreme Dharma characterized by meditation upon Me, worship, service, and glorification—which cannot be properly promulgated by anyone other than Me—may be established in its true form.
The meaning is "in order to establish.
"In age after age" means in every age or in every kalpa.
And thus, there is no partiality on the part of the Blessed One resulting from the subduing of the wicked.
This is not to be doubted.

Even for wicked asuras, that punishment—which delivers them from saṃsāra by means of their own execution at the hands of the Creator, thereby averting the various fruits of their evil deeds and the torments of hell—is indeed determined to be nothing other than a favor. //8//

Baladeva said: "Indeed, even royal sages who are Your devotees are capable of removing the decline of dharma and the rise of adharma; for what purpose, then, do You appear? To this He replied with the word "pari-": for the protection of the virtuous (*sādhu*)—those devoted to My form and qualities—who long for direct perception of Me and are exceedingly distressed in its absence, from the suffering consisting of that very distress;

and likewise, for the sake of those evildoers (*duṣkṛt*), performers of wicked deeds such as the ten-headed Rāvaṇa and Kaṃsa, who cannot be slain by others than Me and who are hostile to such devotees, [by means of My most enchanting personal manifestation].

The destruction of dharma—characterized by worship and meditation upon Me alone, namely pure bhakti-yoga, which is Vedic and impossible for anyone other than Me to propagate—and its establishment, that is, its thorough dissemination; these three are the causes of My manifestation.
Furthermore, there is no partiality on the part of Hari, as He slays the wicked in each age according to the requirements of that particular time.
For, when those who are wicked attain the bliss of liberation, it transforms into a form of grace toward them. //8//
O Arjuna, he who knows in truth thus my divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, does not come to rebirth; he comes to Me. (4.9)
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of knowing such births and activities of the Lord in the verse beginning with "janma.

He who knows that my birth and activity—performed by my own will and consisting of the protection of dharma—are divine (*divya*, i.e., super-mundane) and in reality intended solely for the sake of favoring others, abandons the conceit of the body and does not go, that is, does not attain, to rebirth in *saṃsāra*.
But he reaches Me alone. //9//
Madhusūdana:
My birth is merely a playful imitation of that which is eternally established for Me, who am a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss.

And My action—namely, the protection of the world through the establishment of Dharma—is divine and non-material for Me, the eternally established Lord; it is impossible for others to perform and is unique to the Lord alone.
He who understands in its true essence, through the removal of delusion, that which has been established by the passage beginning with "Thus, though unborn," [perceives the truth].

For by the foolish, through the error of [perceiving] mortality, even the Lord's birth in the form of dwelling in a womb and so forth has been superimposed as being for the sake of his own enjoyment and as resulting from karma;

having dispelled that [superimposition] by means of the knowledge that His nature is, in the ultimate sense, pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss, there is the imitation of birth by the Unborn through Māyā.

Even for one who is not the performer of the action, there is the imitation of that action for the sake of favoring others; he who knows this, through the dawning of the reality of the Self, leaves behind this body and does not undergo rebirth.
Rather, he goes to Me alone—the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—and is liberated from saṃsāra; this is the meaning. //9//
Viśvanātha:
He says "janma" (birth) etc., meaning that one would achieve the goal of life merely by knowing in truth the birth and the subsequent deeds of me, whose characteristics have been described above.
Śrī Rāmānujācārya and the venerable feet of Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī explain "divyam" as non-material (*aprākṛtam*).
"Divya means 'extraordinary' (alaukika)," says Śrī-Svāmī-Caraṇa.

Since the worlds are created from material nature (prakṛti), the meaning of the word "extraordinary" intended by him is precisely its being non-material (aprākṛta). Therefore, because they transcend the modes of nature due to their non-material nature, the births and activities of the Lord are eternal.
And that [birth] does not exist in the composition of the Blessed One; this has been established by the venerable Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī in the verse *yasya ca janma karma vā* (BhP 8.3.8).
Alternatively, even if it is not logically consistent, this should be understood as being beyond reasoning (*atarka*) due to the authority of the words of the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

In that regard, in the Pippalāda recension, there is the *Puruṣabodhinī-śruti*: "The one God, eternally enamored of His pastimes, pervading His devotees, is the inner Self within the hearts of His devotees."

Likewise, the eternality of my birth and activities has been extensively elaborated in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*. Thus, in my own words— specifically in the passages beginning with "He who knows this in truth," "Though being unborn and of imperishable nature," and "And my birth and activities are divine"— one should, through faith (*āstikatā*), understand my birth and activities.
The meaning is that one who knows only their eternity, without even requiring any logical justification for the eternity of those two;
or alternatively, as it is stated in the *Gītā* (17.23): "In truth, the threefold designation of Brahman is remembered as Om, Tat, and Sat."

By the word "that" (tat) mentioned previously, Brahman is meant; its state is "reality" (tattvam). Thus, the meaning is: he who knows by way of that nature of Brahman—having abandoned his current body—he does not undergo rebirth, but rather comes to Me alone.
They have explained it thus because of the addition of the phrase "having abandoned the body."
Having cast off this body, he does not undergo rebirth; rather, even without casting off the body, he comes to Me.

By means of the thorough knowledge of the true nature of My divine birth and activities, all the sins that oppose taking refuge in Me are destroyed; thus, in this very life, having taken refuge in Me in the manner described, being My sole beloved and having his mind fixed on Me alone, he attains Me—so say the venerable feet of Śrī Rāmānujācārya. 9.

Baladeva: With the intention, "May liberation—which is difficult to attain even through thousands of means involving great exertion—be easily accessible to those who follow the path of my single-minded devotees simply by hearing the account of my births," the Blessed Lord said, "My birth," etc., meaning:
of me, the Lord of all, whose will is ever true, and who possesses manifold forms such as Nṛsiṃha and Raghunātha that are eternally established like [the gem] vaidūrya.
In each respective place, the birth and the deeds described by their characteristics— those connected with His various devotees—
are both divine, non-material, and eternal; he who knows this truly as it is,
that He is the one God who is eternally devoted to His pastimes, pervading His devotees and dwelling within the hearts of His devotees, who has been in the past and will be in the future.
O Arjuna, one who possesses firm faith through the Vedic scripture stating "the inner self" and through my own words "the divine," being independent of logical reasoning,
leaves behind this present body and does not undergo birth again in the realm of phenomenal existence.
However, the meaning is that one becomes liberated when one approaches Me alone, who am pleasing through those various actions;

or else, it should be explained as: "He who knows My birth and actions in their true essence as being Brahman, according to the Vedic text 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi), which serves as a sign of My power to liberate."
Otherwise, the scriptural passage—"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8)—would be contradicted.
The rest is the same.
As for the logical arguments regarding the eternity of birth and so forth, they should be sought elsewhere in detail. //9//

Those whose passion, fear, and anger have departed, who are absorbed in Me, and who have taken refuge in Me— many such people, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state of being. 10.10
Śrīdhara: How can there be attainment of you through knowledge of [my] birth and actions? To this he says: "by one free from passion" (vīta-rāga).
Having understood my supreme compassion—that I perform the protection of the Dharma through incarnations of pure being (śuddha-sattva)—[one attains me].
Having taken refuge in Me alone,
they possess self-knowledge and austerity obtained through My grace;
their own duty (svadharma) is the cause for the ripening of that [knowledge and austerity].

The state of those two [knowledge and austerity] combined as a single unit is expressed by the compound *jñāna-tapas*. By that knowledge and austerity, they were purified—that is, cleansed—having cast off the impurities of ignorance and its effects;
many have thus attained my own state, which is union with me (*matsāyujya*).
The meaning is that this path of devotion to Me has not only just begun.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "I know all those," having demonstrated the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*—namely the Lord (*īśvara*) and the individual soul (*jīva*)—through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of knowledge and ignorance respectively;

and having shown that the Lord is eternally pure due to the absence of ignorance, while for the individual soul ignorance is removed through the knowledge obtained by the grace of the Lord; [the following is stated].
It should be understood that it has been stated that for one who is pure, there is identity with the aspect of consciousness (cid-aṃśa). //10//
Madhusūdana:

By saying "He comes to me, O Arjuna," he demonstrates here his own status as the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*)—being attainable by all who are liberated—as well as the fact that this path to liberation has been handed down through an eternal succession. [In the phrase] "one whose passion has departed" (*vīta-rāga*), *rāga* refers to the thirst for various respective fruits.

The fear that "having abandoned all sense-objects, how shall one live on the path of knowledge? is *trāsa*. The anger that "this path of knowledge, which cuts off all sense-objects, how could it be beneficial? is *krodha*.

Those from whom these—attachment, fear, and anger—have departed (*vīta*) through discernment (*viveka*), being gone away from them, are those whose attachment, fear, and anger have departed; they are pure beings (*śuddha-sattva*).

"Many—meaning numerous—have attained My state, that is, they have become one with Me, the Supreme Self, through knowledge-asceticism; for knowledge itself is asceticism because it is the cause of the destruction of all karma.
For, as He will say later: 'Indeed, there is nothing here in this world as purifying as knowledge.'"
Purified by that [knowledge], with all their sins destroyed, and having cast off the impurities of ignorance and its effects, they have attained my state—
that is, my own nature, which is a mass of pure being, consciousness, and bliss, liberation.
They have reached liberation simply through the removal of ignorance.
"Purified by the austerity of knowledge, being liberated while alive (jīvanmukta), they have attained my state—that is, a state directed toward me—known as *rati*, which is love.
For he will later say: "Among them, the man of knowledge, who is constantly disciplined and possesses single-minded devotion, is distinguished" (7.17). //10//
Viśvanātha:

Not only is it the case that a single person of the present day attains Me merely by knowing the truth of My birth and activities; rather, those of the past as well—those who possessed knowledge of the truth of My birth and activities as I descended in each preceding kalpa—also attained Me.
"They have indeed attained [Me]," He says, "having crossed over [the world].

Śrī Rāmānujācārya’s venerable feet explain that *tapas* is knowledge—characterized by the aforementioned definition—which consists precisely in the true experience of My birth and activities; they are purified by that.

Alternatively, it refers to the austerity consisting in the endurance of the burning poison of the serpents of various false doctrines and fallacious arguments regarding the ascertainment of the eternality of My birth and activities within that knowledge; they are purified by that.

And so says the Śruti cited by the venerable Rāmānuja: "The wise know its source" (*tasya dhīrāḥ parijānanti yonim*). This means that only the wise (*dhīrāḥ*), that is, those possessed of intelligence, know its source, which is the manner of its birth.

Those from whom passion and the like have been cast away—meaning those who have no attachment, no affection, nor fear toward people who chatter with evil opinions, and likewise no anger toward them—are my devotees.
Why? Because they are absorbed in me (*man-mayāḥ*), being rich in meditation upon, reflection on, hearing of, and chanting about my births and deeds.
"Mad-bhāvam" means love for me. //10//

Baladeva: To confirm the eternity of My births and so forth—showing that even in the past, as now, the liberation of many occurred through the knowledge of the eternality of My births and so forth—the Lord says, "Vīta... (XIII.25).
The connection [of the verse] is: "In the past, many people, having become purified by knowledge and austerity, attained My state.
That very knowledge concerning the eternality of My births and so forth is [the means], because it is to be accomplished through the Vedas and reasoning which are difficult to master.

The meaning is: by that austerity (tapas)—which, in the case of either [physical] austerity or knowledge, consists in the warding off of various false doctrines, fallacious arguments, and so forth—they are purified, which is to say, their ignorance has been shaken off.
"Devotion toward me" (mayi bhāvam) means love, or presence, or direct realization of Me.
To the question "What are they like?", he says: "vītā...
etc. Those by whom attachment and the like—which are opposed to that permanence—have been discarded (vītāḥ) are [the ones referred to];
the meaning is that they do not manifest attachment toward them, nor fear, nor anger.
The reason for this is: they have taken refuge in me, being devoted to me alone, and are constantly serving me. (10)
In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them;
O Pārtha, human beings follow My path in every respect. (4.11)
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But then, is there partiality even in you?
For you grant the dissolution of the self only to those who have you as their sole refuge, and not to others who possess desires.
To this, he says: "He... (yaḥ).
Just as and in whatever manner—whether with desire or without desire—those who worship Me, I likewise worship them by bestowing the fruits they expect, and thereby favoring them.
It should not be thought that I am indifferent toward those who, abandoning Me, worship Indra and others simply because they possess desires;
for in every way and in all respects, even the servants of Indra and the other gods follow my very path, the path of worship.
Because even in the form of Indra and others, it is I alone who am to be served. //11//
Madhusūdana:

[Objection: "Indeed, those who are purified by knowledge and austerity and are free from desire attain Your state, whereas those who are unpurified and possess desire do not; thus, there would be partiality and cruelty on Your part as the giver of fruits. To this, He says, "Those who [worship] in whatever way... and so forth, to show that it is not so.

In whatever manner— whether with desire or without desire— those who are distressed, those seeking wealth, those desiring knowledge, and those already possessing knowledge take refuge in and worship Me, the Lord and giver of all fruits, I likewise worship them— that is, I favor them— by granting exactly the fruits they seek, and not otherwise.

In this regard, I favor those who do not seek liberation—those afflicted by suffering and those seeking material wealth—by removing their suffering and granting them their objects of desire. I favor those who seek knowledge—those who perform desireless actions as prescribed by such Vedic injunctions as "they desire to know through sacrifice"—by granting them knowledge; and I favor those wise ones who seek liberation by granting them liberation. The meaning is that I do not grant anything other than what is desired to those who desire something else.
[Objection: "But even so, you grant the fruit only to your own devotees and not to the devotees of other deities; thus, partiality remains established. [Reply:
No, for they follow my path—the way of devotion characterized by action and knowledge—of me, Vāsudeva, the Self of all.
O Pārtha, humans who are omniscient follow Indra and the others in every respect, yet they follow me as well.
Thus, regarding those entitled to perform ritual actions:

based on the wording of mantras such as "They call Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni," and according to the principle stated in *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 3.2.38, "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical," the meaning is that the Blessed Lord alone is the giver of fruits in every form whatsoever.
And so he will say: "Even those who are devotees of other deities" [Gītā 9.23], and so forth. //11//
Viśvanātha:

Now, it may be argued that those who are exclusively devoted to You certainly believe in the eternality of Your births and activities; however, some such as the *jñānis* and others, who have taken refuge in You for the sake of attaining knowledge and other perfections, do not believe in the eternality of Your births and activities. To this, He says: "He who... (verse 10).
In whatever manner they approach and worship me, in that very same manner I also worship them;
that is, I bestow the fruit of their devotion.
This is the meaning: those who, keeping in mind that the birth and activities of my Lord are indeed eternal, [engage] in His respective pastimes...

Thus, those who worship me with their special desires fulfilled bring me joy; and I too, by virtue of my sovereignty, am capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise. I can even make their births and actions eternal, having made them my own attendants, appearing together with them at the appropriate time and withdrawing again, while bestowing grace upon them at every moment.
I grant them only that love which is the fruit of worshipping Me. Even those such as the *jñānis* who, considering My births and deeds to be perishable and My form to be composed of *māyā*,
take refuge in Me— I too [lead] them again and again [back to the cycle], for they possess perishable births and deeds and have fallen into the snares of *māyā*.

To those who act in this way, I grant as their fruit only the suffering of birth and death. But those wise ones who, perceiving the eternity of My births and deeds and the nature of My form as being Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (sac-cid-ānanda), take refuge in Me for the sake of attaining self-knowledge—

To those seekers of liberation who desire only the dissolution of their two-fold physical bodies, I grant the fruit of devotion—which is the attainment of imperishable Brahman-bliss—and I bestow the very destruction of birth and death born of ignorance.
Therefore, it is not only My devotees who take refuge in Me;
rather, all human beings in every way—whether they be knowers of truth, performers of action, practitioners of yoga, or worshippers of other deities—do so as well.
And they follow my path because I am the essential nature of all; the meaning is that knowledge, action, and so forth—all is indeed my own path. //11//

Baladeva: [Objection: "But surely You, the Lord of All, are known by me to be eternally possessed of birth and other such qualities; yet another Lord is heard of in scripture as being devoid of birth and so forth, even though He is sometimes described as being the size of a thumb and the like. Therefore, would there not be a duality between You and Your worship? [Reply: To this he says, "Those who... in whatever way," etc. Those devotees who approach and worship Me—the one Lord of All, who, like a cat's-eye gem (*vaidūrya*), appears in many forms—in whatever manner, that is to say, with whatever disposition (*bhāva*), they worship Me.
I, being such as I am, worship them directly with a form and disposition that correspond to their own nature; "bhajan" means I favor them.
The particle *eva* excludes any other possibility.

Therefore, all human beings—out of compassion for the succession of those worshippers who have been engaged in this practice since beginningless time—follow and pursue my path alone, which, though singular, possesses many forms and manifold paths of worship.
Desiring the success of their actions, people here worship the gods;
for in the world of men, success born of action comes quickly. (4.12)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, why do not all people worship you for the sake of liberation alone? To this he says: "Desiring" (kāṅkṣantaḥ). Desiring the success of their actions—that is, the fruit of their actions—people in this world, generally in the human realm, worship only deities such as Indra and others.
But not directly unto Me alone;
for success born of action— that is, the fruit born of action— comes quickly,
whereas the fruit of knowledge, which is liberation (kaivalya), does not.
Because knowledge is difficult to attain. //12//
Madhusūdana:
[To the question,] "Why is it that not everyone takes refuge in You alone, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva?"—He says in response, "kāṅkṣantaḥ" (desiring).

Desiring the success of their actions—that is, the accomplishment of results—in this world, they worship and honor the deities, namely Indra, Agni, and the other gods; because they are obstructed by ignorance, they do not do so while being free from desire.
"Me"—that is, the Blessed One Vāsudeva (this is the ellipsis).

Why? Because for those who sacrifice to deities such as Indra and desire the fruits thereof, the success born of action—the fruit produced by ritual action—occurs quickly, even immediately, in the human world.
However, the fruit of knowledge does not occur quickly, because it depends upon the purification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi).

By the qualification that "the fruit of action manifests quickly in the world of men," the Blessed One has indicated that even in other worlds, the fruits of actions other than those pertaining to the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) are established. Therefore, the meaning is this: because people possessed of desire, being averse to liberation, worship other deities for the sake of attaining various petty fruits, they do not directly take refuge in Me, Vāsudeva, as those seeking liberation do. //12//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, among men, even those who are full of desire, though the path of devotion is manifest before their very eyes, abandon it and instead follow the path of ritual action (*karma-mārga*), which achieves results quickly; thus he says: "Desiring...
and so forth.
Success born of karma consists of heaven and so forth. //12//

Baladeva: Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, and wishing to state that the subject at hand—disinterested action—takes the form of knowledge, he says "kāṅkṣantaḥ" (desiring) to express the rarity of its performance.

In this world, living beings, constrained by the beginningless impressions of enjoyment, desire the success of their actions—the accomplishment of results such as cattle and sons—and worship gods like Indra with rites performed out of desire, rather than worshipping the Lord of all gods.
They worship me—who bestow the fruit of eternal bliss—with those [rites] performed without desire;

for in this human world, success born of action comes quickly. However, from me, when propitiated by selfless action, the success characterized by liberation arises only after a long time, through knowledge.

All people, seized by the latent impressions of worldly enjoyments and lacking discrimination between the real and the unreal, possess a swift desire for enjoyment; therefore, they worship the gods who are my servants for that purpose.

However, no one who possesses discrimination between the real and the unreal worships me, the Lord of all gods, through desireless actions (*niṣkāma-karma*) for the sake of ceasing the suffering of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). The implication is that such a qualified person is rare. //12//
The fourfold social order was created by Me according to the divisions of qualities and actions; know Me to be its author, yet also its non-author, the immutable. 13.
Śrīdhara: But surely there is a diversity of actions, for some engage in action with desire while others do so without desire;
and since you ordain the distinctions of superior, middling, and so forth among the Brahmins and other castes who perform those acts, how is it that you are not subject to partiality?
Anticipating this objection, he says "the fourfold caste" (*cāturvarṇyam*).
The term *cāturvarṇyam* means "the four castes themselves"; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
This is the meaning: Brāhmaṇas are those in whom *sattva* predominates; their duties consist of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth.
Kṣatriyas have sattva and rajas as their predominant qualities; their duties consist of valor, warfare, and so forth.
Vaiśyas have rajas and tamas as their predominant qualities; their duties consist of agriculture, commerce, and so forth.
Śūdras have tamas as their predominant quality; their duties consist of service to the three higher varṇas and so forth.
Thus, it is true that the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya) was created by Me alone through the differentiation of qualities and actions;
nevertheless, know Me to be its agent yet, in effect, a non-agent.
The reason for this is: "the Imperishable" (avyayam).
Free from attachment, it is without exertion, or rather, free from destruction and so forth. //13//
Madhusūdana says: "Even due to the inequality of the qualities (guṇas) that initiate the body, not all possess an identical nature; thus he says, 'the fourfold caste' (cāturvarṇyam).
The term 'cāturvarṇya' refers to the four castes themselves; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself."
It was created and produced by the Lord according to the divisions of qualities and actions—that is, according to the divisions of the *guṇas* and the divisions of *karmas*.
For instance, the Brāhmaṇas have *sattva* as their predominant quality, and their actions are *sāttvika*, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*).
The Kṣatriyas have *rajas* as their predominant quality with *sattva* as a subordinate factor, and their actions are likewise characterized by heroism, splendor, and so forth.
The Vaiśyas have tamas as a subordinate factor and rajas as the predominant one, and their activities, such as agriculture and the like, are of that same nature.

The Śūdras have tamas as the predominant factor, and their activities, such as service to the three other castes and so forth, are characterized by tamas; thus they are established in the world of humans.
Anticipating the objection that, in this case, your own partiality is unavoidable because you are the creator of the four castes with their unequal natures—

"No," he said, "know me to be the agent of this fourfold caste system—which is of an unequal nature—only from the perspective of worldly convention; but from the perspective of ultimate reality, know me to be the non-agent, the imperishable, whose greatness is undiminished due to the absence of ego. (13)
Viśvanātha:

But surely, since the paths of devotion and knowledge are liberating while the path of ritual action is binding, a partiality would follow on your part, O Supreme Lord, who are the creator of all paths.
Regarding this, he says "no, no" with respect to the *cāturvarṇya*.
The term *cāturvarṇya* refers simply to the four *varṇas*;
the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
In this regard, the Brāhmaṇas have sattva as their predominant quality; their duties consist of tranquility, self-control, and so forth.

The Kṣatriyas have rajas and sattva as their predominant qualities; their duties consist of valor, warfare, and so forth. The Vaiśyas have tamas and rajas as their predominant qualities; their duties consist of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth.

Those in whom tamas predominates are Śūdras; their duty consists of service. Thus, according to the division of qualities and duties, the four castes were created by me as paths of dharma through the respective divisions of qualities and duties. However, know Me—their author and creator—to be the non-agent and the non-creator.
Because they are created from the qualities of *prakṛti*, and because *prakṛti* is My power,
I am in reality the non-creator even though I am the creator.
The meaning is: "Because my essential nature transcends the qualities of material nature (prakṛti-guṇa).
For this very reason, I am immutable (avyaya).
Even in the capacity of being the creator, there is not even the slightest equality [between us]; such is the sense. //13//

Baladeva: Now, with the two verses beginning with "The fourfold order" (*cāturvarṇyam*), he states the cause for the destruction of the latent impressions of enjoyment which oppose the performance of desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*).

"The fourfold order" (*cāturvarṇyam*) refers to the four castes; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*). Among them, the Brahmins are those in whom *sattva* predominates; their duties are tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.

The Kṣatriyas have rajas and sattva as their predominant qualities; for them, [the duties] are war and so forth. The Vaiśyas have tamas and rajas as their predominant qualities; for them, [the duties] are agriculture and so forth. The Śūdras have tamas as their predominant quality; for them, [the duties] are service to the triad beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. Thus, the four castes, distinguished by these divisions of qualities and divisions of duties, were created by me, the Lord of All.
This is an illustration for both maintenance and dissolution:
"I alone am the agent of the creation and so forth of the phenomenal world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
As the author of the Sūtras said: "From which [Brahman] the birth and so forth of this [world proceed]" (VS 1.1.2).

"Know Me to be the agent of that creation and so forth, yet because I am separated from each respective action, know Me to be a non-agent"—thus He has removed any charge of partiality and the like against Himself. By saying "this is My imperishable nature," the meaning is: even in being the creator, I do not waver because of My equanimity. //13//
"Actions do not taint Me, nor do I have any longing for the fruits of action. He who understands Me thus is not bound by actions. (4.14)
Śrīdhara, demonstrating that very point, says: "Not me.

Even actions such as the creation of the universe do not smear me—that is, they do not cause me to become attached—because I am free from egoism and because I lack any desire for the fruits of action.
"What should be done about the thought that 'they are smearing me'?
For he who knows Me as being free from the taint of action is himself not bound by actions;
for one who knows the cause of My stainlessness—namely, My freedom from egoism, desirelessness, and so forth—his own egoism and other such traits likewise become attenuated. //14//
Madhusūdana:

Actions such as the creation of the universe and so forth do not "smear" me—that is, they do not bind me as the agent who is devoid of egoism and free from the conceit of agency—by virtue of initiating the body.

Having thus refuted agency, he now refutes the state of being an enjoyer: "There is no longing or thirst for the fruit of action on my part," for there is the Vedic scripture: "What longing can there be for one whose desires are fulfilled? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). I am one whose desires are fulfilled.
For actions smear [the agent] through the conceit of agency and the desire for their fruits; because these are absent, actions do not smear me.

Thus, whoever else also recognizes Me as the non-agent and non-enjoyer by virtue of My true nature is not bound by actions; the meaning is that he is liberated through the knowledge of the Self as a non-agent. //14//
Viśvanātha: Let that matter rest for now; you have, however, descended at this time into a Kṣatriya family.
"You perform every day the duties appropriate to the kṣatriya caste; what then is the news regarding that? To this he says: "Not me.
They do not smear, that is, they do not defile me, as if [smearing] a living being.
Nor is there in Me any longing for the fruits of action, such as heaven, as there is for a living soul (jīva).

Even though I am full of My own bliss by virtue of being the Supreme Lord, the intention is that My performance of actions and so forth is solely for the sake of setting the world in motion. Thus [is the meaning of] "Me."
The meaning is that he who does not know is bound by his actions. //14//
Baladeva explains this with the words "na mām" (not me).
Actions such as the creation of the universe and so forth do not "taint" me; that is, they do not stain me with defects such as partiality, as they do a living being.

This is because those actions are prompted by the karma of the living beings to be created, and not by me; furthermore, I have no desire for the fruits of actions such as creation, and therefore they do not taint me.

He who performs actions out of a desire for their fruits is stained by those fruits; I, however, am filled with the bliss of my own essential nature, and having felt compassion arising from the hunger of the individual soul (kṣetrajña) who has dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), I set those actions in motion as a mere instrumental cause, like the rain-cloud. And there is a traditional saying (smṛti): [text follows]

"In the act of creating those things to be created, he is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-mātra*), since the creative powers reside in the primary material cause (*pradhāna*). This and other [passages] state that in the process of creating those *kṣetrajñas* who assume the states of gods, humans, and so forth, this Supreme Lord is merely the efficient cause.
The meaning is this: rather, it is the potencies of the past karma of those beings to be created that serve as the cause for the diversity of states such as gods and so forth.
Thus the author of the Sūtras says, beginning with: "Because of partiality and cruelty" (VS 2.1.35).
Thus he states the fruit of this knowledge: "He who fully knows Me as I am"—
such a person is not bound by past karmas, which are the causes of bondage and are opposed to that [knowledge].
The meaning is that one is liberated by means of them. //14//
Knowing this, even the seekers of liberation of old performed action;
therefore, you too perform action, which was performed by the ancients long ago. (4.15)

Śrīdhara: Having dispelled the incidental objection regarding the partiality of the Lord with the four verses beginning with "In whatever way they [worship Me]," He now recalls and elaborates upon the previously mentioned *karma-yoga* with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Action performed while free from egoism and other such defects does not lead to bondage.
Knowing this, even those seekers of liberation in the past, such as Janaka and others, performed ritual action first, even in previous ages, for the sake of purifying the mind;
therefore, you too should perform action first. //15//
Madhusūdana:

Since one is not bound by actions due to the knowledge that "I am not the doer" and "I have no longing for the fruits of action," he says "thus" (evam). Having thus known the non-attachment of the non-doing Self to action, [action] was performed even by those seekers of liberation in this age who have passed away, such as Yayāti, Yadu, and others.

Therefore, you too should perform action alone—neither remaining silent nor practicing renunciation. If you are not a knower of reality, then act for the sake of self-purification; if you are a knower of reality, then act for the sake of maintaining the world.
This was performed by the ancients, such as Janaka and others, first, earlier, and even more anciently in other ages.
By this, he shows that because it was performed by those who came before and even further back in this age and other ages, you must necessarily perform the action. //15//
Viśvanātha:
Having known Me to be exactly as I am described, even the ancients such as Janaka and others performed action solely for the sake of setting an example for the world. //15//
Baladeva: "So it is.
Having known Me alone, My ancient disciples who followed Me—Vivasvat and the others—performed action free from desire while seeking liberation.
Therefore, you too should perform that very same action.
It is not a renunciation of action.
The meaning is: if one's mind is impure, it is for the sake of purifying the mind which contains the essence of knowledge; if the mind is already pure, it is for the sake of gathering the world.
Of what kind was that which was performed by those predecessors?
Earlier; very ancient. //15//
"What is action? What is inaction?"—even the wise are bewildered by this question.
Therefore, I shall declare to you that action, knowing which you will be liberated from evil. (4.16)

Śrīdhara: And that must be performed after deliberating with those who know reality, not merely by following worldly tradition; thus he asks, "What is action?"—meaning, what is the nature of the performance of action?
