"What is action? What is the nature of non-action?"—in this matter even the discerning are deluded.

Therefore, I shall explain to you that which is action and that which is non-action, by knowing and performing which you will be liberated from the inauspicious cycle of worldly existence; listen to that. 16.
Madhusūdana:

Now, is there indeed some doubt regarding the subject of action, such that you press so persistently with the words "What is action?"—claiming that it was performed by the ancients in even earlier times?
He says "What is action? precisely because such a doubt certainly exists.

Because one standing on a boat perceives the illusion of motion even in stationary trees on the bank, and because from a distance one perceives the illusion of non-motion even in men who are moving when they are close to the eye— regarding what is truly action and what is truly non-action in this matter, even the wise and intelligent have been deluded; that is, they have fallen into a state of confusion characterized by an inability to reach a definitive conclusion.
The meaning is "because it is extremely difficult to define.

Therefore (tat), for that reason, I shall declare (pravakṣyāmi) to you (te) both action (karma) and, by eliding the letter 'a' (akāra-praśleṣeṇa) and thus cutting [the compound], non-action (akarma); that is, I shall declare them thoroughly (prakarṣeṇa) by way of severing all doubt.
Having known that action which is in the nature of inaction, you shall be liberated—you will be freed—from the evil of saṃsāra. //16//
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, even action should not be performed by a discerning person merely by following the maxim of "going where others have gone";
rather, it must be done only after knowing its specific mode. Therefore, he states that this [mode] is difficult to understand at the outset. //16//

Baladeva: If it is asked, "Is there indeed some doubt regarding action, such that you speak with such persistence, saying that what was done by the ancients was done even more so by those before them?"—the answer is that there certainly is.
He says this in the words, "What is action?

(18.1). The meaning is: what would be the nature of the action to be performed by those seeking liberation, and what is the nature of non-action—which is distinct from action—and also the knowledge contained therein?

And regarding its difference from that [action], even wise poets have been deluded in this matter; they fell into delusion because of their inability to determine its true nature. I, the Lord of all and the All-knowing, shall declare to you that action—which, through the elision of the letter *a*, is "non-action"—by knowing which, and by performing and attaining which, you will be liberated from the evil of saṃsāra. //16//
For one must understand action, and one must understand what is contrary to action, and one must understand inaction; the way of action is profound. (4.17)

Śrīdhara: But surely, action (karman) is well-known in the world as consisting of the activities of the body and so forth, while inaction (akarma) consists of the absence of such activity; therefore, how can it be said that even the wise have fallen into delusion regarding this?
Regarding this, he says "of action" (karmaṇaḥ).
The true nature (tattva) of action—even that which consists of prescribed activity—is to be understood;
it is not merely what is commonly known in the world.
The true nature of *akarma*— even that which is not a prescribed activity— must be understood; likewise, the true nature of *vikarma*— even that which is a prohibited activity— must be understood,
because the course of action is profound.
The mention of "action" (karman) is intended as an illustration;
the meaning is that the true nature of action, inaction, and mis-action is difficult to discern. //17//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: "Indeed, because this is well-known to all the world, I myself know that the activity of the body, senses, and so forth is action (*karman*), whereas sitting silently is inaction (*akarma*); what, then, is there for you to say in that regard? To this, he says:
"Of action... (*karmaṇaḥ*).
For indeed, the true nature must be understood even of action prescribed by the scriptures,
as well as of "vikarman" (forbidden action),
and of "akarman" (inaction), which is the state of remaining silent.
In all three of these statements, the phrase "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Because [the nature of] action is profound and difficult to understand— where "action" is an elliptical expression for action, inaction, and mis-action.
The meaning is that the goal is the reality. //18//
Viśvanātha:
The truth is that the performance of prohibited acts leads to an evil destiny.
Likewise, regarding the non-performance of action by a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), what kind of non-performance of action is auspicious?
The sense is: otherwise, how could the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) come into one's grasp? The term "of action" (karmaṇaḥ) is an elliptical expression for action, inaction, and mis-action.
"Gati" means the true nature (tattva).
They are dense and difficult to traverse. //17//
Baladeva: If it be objected that even poets have fallen into delusion, he says in response: "For [the nature] of action...
One must understand the true nature of *niṣkāma* (disinterested) action, which is to be performed by those seeking liberation;
and one must understand the true nature of *vikarman* (misdeed), which is desire-driven action contrary to knowledge.
The true nature of both actionless knowledge—which is distinct from action—and of action itself must be understood;
the meaning is that this should be investigated together with those who know their respective natures.
The course of both action and non-action is profound and difficult to traverse.
Therefore, even the poets are deluded regarding that. //17//
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. (18)
Śrīdhara: Thus, demonstrating that action and the other factors are difficult to discern, he says, "In action.

Regarding action—characterized by the propitiation of the Supreme Lord—one who perceives "non-action" in action, meaning "this is not action," for him there is no bondage because it serves as a cause for knowledge.
And he who perceives action even in non-action—that is, in the non-performance of prescribed duties—because it is a cause of bondage by producing transgression;
among men performing actions, he is wise because he possesses a resolute intellect, and is therefore superior.
The Lord praises him: "He is disciplined; he is a yogi."
By that action, one attains the yoga of knowledge;
he alone is the performer of all actions,
because within that action— which is like a reservoir overflowing with water— all the fruits of every action are included.

Thus, for one who desires to ascend [to yoga], the very *karma-yoga* that was previously stated in the passage beginning with "not by abstaining from actions" has been clarified in this state of eligibility for *karma-yoga*.
Furthermore, because this section is an expansion (*prapañca*) of that [teaching], there is no fault of redundancy.

By this very [verse], the elaboration of that non-involvement in action which was stated for the stage of one who has ascended to yoga—beginning with "he should be one who delights only in the Self"—should be understood as being established by implication. Furthermore, this verse is also applicable here: if even for one desiring to ascend, action does not become a cause of bondage, how much less so for one who has already ascended? Could it possibly be a cause of bondage?

Alternatively, even while the activity of the body, senses, and so forth is occurring, he who perceives non-action— that is, the natural state of *niṣkarmya*— through the experience of the Self's distinction from the body and other such things; and likewise, he who perceives action within non-action— that is, in the renunciation of actions due to the perception of them as suffering because they lack knowledge— [perceives correctly], for [the latter] is a false practice since it is achieved through mere effort.
This has been stated in the passage beginning with "having restrained the organs of action," and so forth.
One who is thus constituted is the wise and learned man among all human beings.

The reason for this is as follows: even while performing all actions—such as eating and the like—which have come about by chance, he remains truly disciplined (*yukta*); that is to say, through the knowledge of the Self as a non-agent, he remains established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

By this very [principle], it should be understood that for the knower, the consumption of *kalañja* and so forth—which occurs spontaneously due to his own nature—is not a fault; however, for the ignorant person, what is done out of passion is a fault. Thus, the true nature of even "forbidden action" (*vikarman*) is to be discerned. //18//
Madhusūdana:

What, then, is the true nature of action and the rest? To this he says, "In action" (*karmaṇi*). Action refers to the activity of the body, senses, and so forth, whether enjoined or prohibited; it is superimposed upon the Self through the false attribution of agency (*dharmy-adhyāsa*), thinking "I am doing."

Just as one standing on a boat might superimpose motion upon the trees on the bank while they are actually stationary, so too does one who perceives the absence of action in reality— due to the failure to discern the nature of the non-acting Self— see [action where there is none], as in the case of those trees; likewise, when the cessation of activity (inactivity) is superimposed upon the body, senses, and so forth— which are always engaged in operation as transformations of the *māyā* of the three *guṇas*— by means of the conceit that "I remain inactive, silent, and at ease," [he sees] in those persons situated nearby who are actually observing with their eyes from a distance.

Even while moving, as if there were no movement, he who— by constantly reflecting on the true nature of the body, senses, and so forth, which are characterized by activity— perceives, according to the actual state of things, that the action consisting of effort called "cessation" is present, just as one perceives movement in the aforementioned persons;
even in a state of indifference, he thinks, "I was indifferent."
Arrogance itself is action.
By the words "such a one who perceives the ultimate truth is wise," and so forth, he is praised through three attributes: being wise, being endowed with yoga, and performing all actions.
Here, by the first quarter-verse, the true nature of both action (*karman*) and non-action (*vikarman*) is established, because the word *karman* refers here to both prescribed and prohibited acts.
It should be understood that the second quarter of the verse demonstrates the true nature of actionlessness (*akarma*).
In this regard, your thought—that because action is a cause of bondage, you should remain silent and at ease—is false;
for when the conceit of agency is absent, there is no quality of action—whether enjoined or prohibited—that constitutes a cause of bondage.

And thus it has been explained by the passage beginning with, “Actions do not smear me” (Gītā 4.14). Even that action consisting of the conceit of indifference, such as thinking “I remained silent,” is indeed a cause of bondage when there is the conceit of agency, because of the failure to understand the true nature of reality.

Therefore, having understood the true nature of action, prohibited action, and inaction in this way, and having abandoned both prohibited action and inaction, you should perform only prescribed action, through the relinquishing of the conceit of agency and the desire for fruits.
The intention [of the verse] is as follows:

another explanation is that he who, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭyā*), perceives that which is non-action (*akarma*) and unknowable (*avedya*), yet is self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-caitanya*); which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all delusions; and which is woven through (*anusyūta*) the object of action—the visible, insentient world—both as its being (*sad-rūpa*) and its manifestation (*sphuraṇa-rūpa*).

Likewise, action is superimposed upon the self-luminous object of vision; this visible world is composed of illusion (*māyā*) and is not ultimately real, because a relationship between the seer and the seen is logically untenable—as it is said:
"He who perceives all beings as indeed within his own Self..."
And because he sees himself in all beings, he does not feel aversion toward them.
Thus says the Śruti (Īśa Upaniṣad 6).
Therefore, even amidst this mutual superimposition, he alone among men who perceives the pure reality is truly wise, and no other;
for he possesses the vision of the ultimate truth, whereas the other possesses the vision of that which is not the ultimate truth.
And he, being endowed with the fitness for the means of attaining wisdom, possesses a mind that is pure and one-pointed through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Therefore, he alone is praised by his actual qualities as "one who has performed all actions that are the means for purifying the internal organ.
Since this is so, the intention is that you too should become a seer of the ultimate truth; for by that alone, the state of performing all actions is appropriately established.
Therefore, that which was said— "Knowing which, you shall be liberated from the inauspicious"—
and that which was said regarding the reality of karma and so forth, as well as the praise beginning with "he is wise," all of that is consistent with the vision of ultimate truth.
Since liberation from the impure cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is impossible through any knowledge other than [knowledge of reality],
and since that which is other than reality is neither to be understood nor constitutes wisdom even when known, the explanation of those who perceive the ultimate truth is indeed correct.
As for the explanation that this is "non-action" (*akarma*) because it lacks the cause of bondage when performed as a constant duty for the sake of the Supreme Lord— [that is not so].

Likewise, the statement that "he who perceives this action as action—even in the non-performance of obligatory duty (*nitya-karman*)—because it is a cause for transgression (*pratyavāya*), is wise," and so forth, is entirely inconsistent.
This is because the knowledge that "this is non-action" regarding obligatory duty cannot be a cause for liberation from evil;
rather, such knowledge is itself evil, being a form of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
Nor should such false knowledge be understood as the reality; nor is the praise of being "wise" and so forth appropriate for one who possesses such knowledge, because it is erroneous.

Indeed, the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) is useful in its own right by way of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); however, the notion that they are non-action (*akarma-buddhi*) is of no use whatsoever, because it is not enjoined by scripture—just as the meditation on Name and so forth as Brahman (*brahma-dṛṣṭi*) is not [enjoined] in this context.
Nor does this very statement enjoin that [view], because it has been stated that it contradicts the introductory passages and other criteria;

likewise, even the non-performance of obligatory rites (nitya-karma) serves to indicate an action contrary in nature to the obligatory rite, but the perception of ritual action (karma-dṛṣṭi) therein is of no use whatsoever.
Nor does sin accrue from the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*),
because an entity cannot arise from non-existence;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the production of effects at all times, since that [non-existence] is without distinction.

According to the principle that "words denoting action have being as their meaning; from them, action is understood, for this is what is enjoined," it is the meaning consisting of an action (*bhāvārtha*) alone that produces the unseen potency (*apūrva*). This is because even in cases such as "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," it is accepted that a specific mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) alone produces the *apūrva*, just like the vows of Prajāpati such as "one should not look at the rising sun."

Therefore, at a time when the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) is required, any action such as sitting down that is contrary to those rites is itself the cause of sin (*pratyavāya*), characterized by the non-performance of the obligatory rite; this is the view of the Vaidikas.

For this very reason, in the passage "not performing the enjoined rite" (*akurvan vihitaṃ karma*), the suffix *śatṛ* is explained in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Even though there is an undifferentiated traditional rule stating "of an action [used] in the sense of a characteristic or a cause" (*lakṣaṇa-hetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*), a causal sense (*hetutva*) is untenable here.
Therefore, while the removal of false vision (*mithyā-darśana*) is the subject at hand, an exposition of false vision is by no means appropriate.
Nor does this statement— "he who [sees] inaction in action"— have as its sole purpose the constant performance of obligatory rites in the sense that "one should perform the obligatory duties."

The statement beginning with "one would see" and so forth has been explained at length in the Bhāṣya itself, on the grounds that the Blessed One would incur the charge of being a deceiver by employing such a statement which fails to convey that [reality]; therefore, we shall desist. //18//
Viśvanātha:
Regarding that, he speaks of the realization of the truth concerning action and inaction with the words "In action...

Even for one of pure internal organ who possesses knowledge, when performing action—such as Janaka and others—without having formally renounced, there is "inaction" within the yoga of desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*).

The sense is this: he who perceives that "this is not action" [does so] because that action lacks the quality of being a cause of bondage. Likewise, even though one whose internal organ is impure lacks true knowledge, a renunciant who merely prattles about knowledge—despite his learning in the scriptures—perceives non-action (the failure to perform action) as action; he regards it as nothing other than a bondage of action that leads to an evil state.
He alone is truly wise;
he performs all actions indeed,
but the meaning is that even through association with, or even by the words of, that talkative knower who merely fancies himself a knower, one does not abandon [action].
And thus says the word of the Blessed One: "But he who has not restrained the group of six, whose charioteer is the fierce senses,
and who is devoid of knowledge and dispassion, merely lives off the triple staff."

"The destroyer of dharma, whose impurities are not yet ripened, denies the gods, the Self, that which resides within the Self, and Me; because of this, he is deprived of both this world and the next. [BhP 11.18.40-1] //18//
Baladeva: He states the essential nature of action and inaction that is to be understood with the words "In action...

One who perceives inaction within action—that is, self-knowledge within the desireless action being performed—and one who perceives action within inaction—that is, ritual action within self-knowledge.

This is what is meant: the seeker of liberation should perceive that action performed for the purification of the heart is of the nature of knowledge because it contains within it the pursuit of self-knowledge; and he should perceive that very knowledge is of the nature of action because it has action as its means.
The meaning is that one should know both to be one, since they both have the single goal of the Self.
In this very way, it will be stated [in the Gītā] starting with the words, "The ignorant speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as distinct.
When action is performed in this manner, he who contemplates the true nature of the Self among men is wise and learned;
he is disciplined and fit for liberation.
He is the performer of all actions because the fruits of all actions are included within the bliss of self-knowledge. //18//
The wise call him a learned man whose every undertaking is free from desire and purposeful resolve, and whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. (4.19)

Śrīdhara: By means of the scriptural statement "He who sees inaction in action" and through logical implication (*arthāpatti*), that very pair of meanings has been stated; he clarifies that same point with the five verses beginning with "Of whom...
Actions are called *samārambha* because they are properly undertaken.
That which is desired is *kāma*, meaning the fruit [of action].
They call him wise who is devoid of the mental resolve for those [actions].

The reason for this is that when the mind is purified, his actions—burnt by the fire of knowledge born therefrom—are reduced to a state of non-action (*akarmatā*). However, in the stage of one who has ascended [to yoga], desire has as its object the fruit, the cause, and the field of action.
The resolve regarding what is to be done is the thought that "this must be performed for that purpose.
They are devoid of these two.
The rest is clear. //19//
Madhusūdana:

This state of being untainted by action due to the absence of the conceit of agency in one who perceives the supreme reality is now elaborated upon, from the verse beginning with "He for whom all... up to the end of the section on "the meditative absorption in Brahman as action" (*brahma-karma-samādhi*).
For that aforementioned perceiver of the supreme reality, whatever undertakings there may be—whether Vedic or worldly—are undertaken.

According to this etymology, "actions" refers to those that are free from desire and mental resolve. Desire is thirst for the fruit; mental resolve is the egoistic conceit of agency, thinking "I am the doer.

Actions devoid of these two become mere futile exertions, undertaken either for the sake of maintaining worldly order, for the sake of mere livelihood, or due to the momentum of previously commenced karma (*prārabdha-karma*).

The vision of action as non-action and so forth regarding that [action] is knowledge; that itself is the fire. By that fire are burnt the actions characterized as auspicious and inauspicious for one who has attained it.

This is because of the principle stated in the *Nyāya-sūtra* (4.1.13): "Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging of future [actions] and the destruction of past [actions], as designated by those terms."
The wise, who know Brahman, call him a true scholar in the ultimate sense whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge;
for it is one who possesses right vision who is called a scholar, not one who is deluded—this is the meaning. //19//
Viśvanātha:
He explains the aforementioned meaning with five verses beginning with "yasya" (of whom). "Samārambhāḥ" refers to actions (karmāṇi), so called because they are properly undertaken.

Desire is the fruit; they are devoid of the intention for that [fruit]. Knowledge itself is the fire; by that, the actions—both those prescribed and those prohibited—which are being performed, are burnt away by him who possesses it.
By this, it is also explained that one should understand the case of "wrong action" (*vikarman*) as well.
Just as one who possesses such a qualification should perceive action as inaction, so too should one perceive wrong action as indeed inaction; such is the connection with the preceding verse.
As will be stated further on:
"Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone."
"Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.36–37). //19//
Baladeva: With five verses beginning with "yasya," he describes the form of knowledge that arises from action.

Those who are desired are called *kāmāḥ*, meaning fruits; when one's undertakings—that is, actions—are devoid of, or empty of, the intention for those fruits, and thus become actions dedicated solely to the Self, the wise call such a person a scholar, one who knows the Self.
The reason for this is stated as "jñāna" (knowledge):
he is one whose accumulated karmas have been burnt by the fire of self-knowledge that has become manifest once the heart has been purified through those aforementioned undertakings. //19//
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and dependent on nothing, he does not do anything at all, even though fully engaged in action. (4.20)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "having abandoned" (tyaktvā):
having abandoned attachment to action and its fruit, he is satisfied by his own eternal bliss;
for this very reason, he is devoid of any need to rely on others for the sake of acquisition (yoga) and preservation (kṣema).
The meaning is that for one who has become thus, even though engaged fully in natural or prescribed action, he does not do anything at all; for him, action attains the state of non-action. //20//
Madhusūdana:

Let it be granted that past *karmas* not yet commenced are burnt by the fire of knowledge and that future ones do not arise. However, someone might raise the doubt: "But an action performed at the very moment of the arising of knowledge, being included neither among the preceding nor the succeeding [sets of karma], would lead to its own fruit. To dispel this, he says: "Having abandoned... (tyaktvā).

Having abandoned attachment to action and its fruit, as well as the conceit of agency and the desire for enjoyment, and having sublated these through the correct vision of the Self as neither agent nor enjoyer, he is eternally satisfied by the attainment of his own nature as supreme bliss;
thus, he is free from longing for anything whatsoever.

He is "without support" (*nirāśraya*), meaning that from which the support—the body, senses, and so forth—has departed through the realization of non-duality; he is devoid of the conceit of identifying with the body, senses, and other such things.
The two qualifiers [in the verse] are intended sequentially as reasons for the cessation of the desire for fruits and the conceit of agency.

One who is thus liberated while living (jīvanmukta), even when engaged in ritual or worldly action during the state of post-meditative activity (vyutthāna), does not actually do anything from his own perspective, despite appearing to others to be fully engaged in the performance of rites with all their limbs and sub-limbs due to the force of prārabdha-karma; the meaning is that he is sublated by the realization of the actionless Self. //20//
Viśvanātha:
He is eternally satisfied, always satiated by his own bliss; he is without dependence, relying on no one for the sake of his own acquisition or preservation. //20//
Baladeva: He clarifies the meaning already stated with the words "having abandoned" (tyaktvā).

Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, satisfied by the eternal Self experienced [within], and free from dependence—meaning one who is without even the need for support regarding acquisition and preservation—a qualified person such as this, though fully engaged in action, does not do anything at all.
By means of the instruction on the performance of action, he brings about the very culmination in knowledge; this is the stage of one who desires to ascend.
By this, it is stated that the nature of *vikarman* (mis-action) and its binding character must be understood. //20//
Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions,
performing action only for the body, he incurs no sin. (4.21)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "free from desire" (nirāśīḥ): it is one from whom desires—that is, longings—have departed. It refers to one whose mind (citta) and self (ātman)—meaning the body—are restrained (yata) and disciplined (niyata).
He by whom all possessions have been renounced does not incur sin or bondage—even while performing actions that are accomplished by the body alone and are free from the attachment to agency.

In the case of one established in yoga, even while performing natural activities such as wandering for alms which are merely necessary for the maintenance of the body, he does not incur sin, which is the fault arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties. //21//
Madhusūdana:
When even rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma— which are causes of extreme distraction— fail to produce their results by the power of perfect knowledge,
then how could activities such as wandering for alms, which are causes merely for the maintenance of the body and do not cause distraction, ever be a cause of bondage?
Thus, by the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he says: "free from desire" (*nirāśīr*).

One who is free from desire is one whose thirst has departed; one whose mind and self are controlled—where the "mind" (*citta*) is the internal organ and the "self" (*ātman*) is the body together with the external senses, both of which are restrained and subdued by him through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*).

Since his senses are conquered, he is therefore one who has abandoned all possessions (*tyakta-sarva-parigraha*), meaning one by whom all possessions—that is, all objects of enjoyment and their implements—have been relinquished. Because he is free from thirst, he has abandoned everything.

Even such a person, by the force of *prārabdha* karma, performs physical, vocal, and mental actions— such as wearing a loincloth for the mere purpose of maintaining the body, or wandering for alms— which are permitted for an ascetic (*yati*) by the scriptures;
yet he performs even these solely while devoid of the conceit of agency, acting through an agency superimposed by others, because he has realized the Self as ultimately a non-agent.

He does not incur, nor does he attain, *kilbiṣa*—that is, the undesirable *saṃsāra* which is the fruit of *adharma*; for even merit (*puṇya*) is considered *kilbiṣa* because its fruit is likewise undesirable.

As for those who explain *śārīram* as "that which is accomplished by the body," in their view, since the phrase "merely performing action" already suffices, the word *śārīra* would be redundant, as it would provide no additional meaning and fail to serve as a qualification.

Alternatively, if one were to say that [the verse] is intended for the purpose of turning away from vocal and mental [actions], then—since the word *karman* would refer exclusively to what is prescribed—the prohibition "one incurs no sin while performing prescribed bodily action" would be a prohibition of something not applicable, and thus meaningless. Even if [the word *karman*] were intended to include both what is prescribed and what is prohibited, there would likewise be a contradiction; this is explained in detail in the Bhāṣya itself. //21//
Viśvanātha:
The "self" (ātman) refers to the gross body (sthūla-deha).

Even while performing actions such as accepting gifts from the unworthy for the sake of maintaining the body—though this constitutes *vikarman* (misconduct)—one does not incur *kilbiṣa*, that is, sin; this is also to be understood as an explanation of the phrase "and of misconduct."
Baladeva: Now, with three verses beginning with "nirāśīḥ," he describes the state of one who has ascended [to yoga]. "Nirāśīḥ" means one from whom the desire for fruits (*āśīḥ*) has departed.

"Yata-cittātmā" means one who has brought under control both the mind and the body. "Tyakta-sarva-parigraha" means one who has abandoned all possessions because he seeks only the vision of the Self, and is thus devoid of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) toward material objects.
Even while performing bodily action—such as the acquisition of property and so forth—for the sake of maintaining the body, one incurs no sin or evil. //21//
Content with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, free from envy, and equanimous in success and failure— even after acting, such a person is not bound. (4.22)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "attainment by chance" (*yadṛcchā-lābha*):
attainment that presents itself unasked for is "attainment by chance"; one who is content with that is [described as such].
He has transcended, that is, passed beyond, the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat;
the meaning is that he is by nature capable of enduring them.
He is free from envy and devoid of enmity.
One who remains equanimous—free from both joy and dejection—in the attainment or non-attainment of even what is gained by chance;
such a person, having performed prescribed or natural actions on either the preceding or subsequent stages as appropriate, does not incur bondage. //22//
Madhusūdana:
For the ascetic who has renounced all possessions, action is permitted solely for the purpose of maintaining the body;
since the maintenance of the body is impossible without food, clothing, and so forth, one may obtain food and other necessities through begging or by one's own effort.

When it was concluded that [the mendicant] must accomplish [his needs], the author states "obtained by chance" (*yadṛcchā-lābha*) as a restrictive rule. "Chance" (*yadṛcchā*) is the absence of effort not sanctioned by the scriptures; that which is obtained solely through such chance—such as food and clothing that are permitted by the scriptures—is "obtained by chance. One who is content with that and free from craving for more than that is [a true mendicant]. Thus, the scripture, having introduced the rule "he should wander for alms," specifies: "unasked for, unprepared, obtained by chance. This excludes efforts such as begging or making a formal resolve. Manu also says: [Manu 6.58–59] "He should wander for alms at the proper time, avoiding houses he has already visited. He should not be eager for alms, nor should he be indifferent to them. He should collect alms from the houses of those who perform their duties, without being attached to any one family. He should eat what is obtained by chance, without longing for delicacies, and he should never eat food that has been prepared for him."* *(Note: The verse cited here is a reconstruction based on Manu’s intent regarding *yadṛcchā-lābha*.)* Thus, the text prohibits the exertion of begging, making mental resolves, and so forth. "One should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor through instructions or discourses" (Manu 6.50).
Nevertheless, the effort sanctioned by such scriptures as "ascetics enter the village for the sake of alms" must certainly be undertaken.
Thus, even that which is to be obtained is strictly prescribed by the scriptures:
"One should take a pair of loincloths, a garment, a patched cloak to ward off the cold, and also sandals; one should not make a collection of anything else," and so forth.
In this manner, other scriptures consisting of injunctions and prohibitions are also to be inferred.

Now, one might ask: "If [the goal] cannot be attained without one's own effort, how can one who is afflicted by cold, heat, and so forth live? To this he says: "One who has transcended the pairs of opposites" (*dvandvātīta*). The "pairs of opposites" (*dvandva*) are hunger, thirst, cold, heat, rain, and so on; "transcended" (*atīta*) means having gone beyond them, because they do not manifest during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Even when there is a flickering of appearances during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), because these are sublated by the realization of the Self as non-dual supreme bliss, neither agent nor enjoyer, his mind remains undisturbed even while being struck by those pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).

For this very reason, he is free from envy (*vimatsara*); envy (*matsara*) is the desire for one's own excellence preceded by an inability to endure the excellence of others—he is devoid of that, possessing a mind free from enmity through the vision of the non-dual Self.
Consequently, he is equal (*sama*), the same whether there is success or failure in what comes by chance; he is not elated by success, nor dejected by failure.

Dejected by his own experience, he— though not the actual agent, with agency attributed to him by others— even after performing actions such as wandering for alms whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body, is not bound, because action along with its causes, which is the cause of bondage,
has been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Thus is the restatement of what was previously mentioned. //22//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Now, he says "by chance" (*yadṛcchayā*) to show that food, clothing, and so forth for the maintenance of the body should not be procured by one's own effort.
"Chance-gain" (*yadṛcchā-lābha*) is acquisition without begging; one who is "satisfied" (*santuṣṭaḥ*) or content with that [is meant].
One who has transcended dualities such as cold and heat—that is, one who endures them;

one who is free from envy, meaning that even when oppressed by others, he harbors no enmity toward them; and one who is equanimous because there is neither joy at the attainment of gains obtained by chance nor dejection at their non-attainment—one who is thus constituted, even after performing bodily action, is not bound by it.
He is bound, yet by the power of being established in knowledge, he is not defiled. //22//
For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, all karma is completely dissolved. (4.23)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of one whose attachment has gone": this refers to one who is free from desire, liberated from passion and the like;
it refers to one whose mind is established in knowledge.
For one who performs action for the sake of sacrifice—that is, for the sake of the Supreme Lord—the entire action, along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), dissolves;
it attains the state of non-action (*akarma*).
This is said "for the sake of sacrifice" from the perspective of one who has not yet ascended to the stage of yoga.
The meaning is: for the sake of sacrifice—that is, for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice and for the very purpose of maintaining the world—he performs action. //23//
Madhusūdana:

It has been stated that the renunciant (*yati*) who has abandoned all possessions and is content with whatever comes by chance, is not bound even after performing actions such as wandering for alms, which serve solely the purpose of maintaining the body; [the question now arises] regarding the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) who is a householder.
Someone might have the apprehension that the ritual action (karma) performed by Janaka and others, such as sacrifices and the like, could be a cause of bondage;

to dispel this, [the Lord] explains what was stated in the verse beginning with "having abandoned attachment to the fruit of action" by means of the phrase "of one whose attachment has departed. This refers to one who has departed from attachment—that is, one who is devoid of attachment to results—and who is liberated, being free from the superimposition (adhyāsa) of agency, enjoyership, and so forth.

The meaning is: "of one whose mind is established in knowledge," that is, of one whose consciousness remains fixed in the realization of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*), which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
The sequence of successive qualifiers should be understood as being connected by their function as causes for each preceding one.

From where does the state of being free from attachment come? From where does that lack of superimposition (adhyāsa-hīnatva) come? From where does the state of one whose wisdom is established (sthita-prajñatva) come?

Even for such a person, by the force of *prārabdha*-karma, [he acts] "for sacrifice"—meaning for the sake of Viṣṇu or for His pleasure—for the purpose of protecting sacrifice, as an exemplary practice in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, for the sake of setting an example for the world.

For one who performs actions such as sacrifice and charity in their entirety, along with their future fruits—that is, which is "complete"—it "melts away," meaning it dissolves thoroughly through the destruction of its cause by means of the vision of reality (tattva-darśana);
that is to say, it perishes. //23//
Viśvanātha:
Sacrifice (yajña) has the characteristics that will be described hereafter; for one who performs action for its sake, that action dissolves—meaning it attains the state of non-action (akarma). //23//

Baladeva: For one who is free from attachment, devoid of desire, liberated from passion, hatred, and the like, whose mind is absorbed in knowledge concerning the Self, and who performs meditation upon Viṣṇu for the sake of sacrifice to propitiate Him, all prior karma that causes bondage is entirely and completely dissolved. //23//
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the yoga of action that is Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained. (4.24)
Śrīdhara: Thus, action characterized by the worship of the Supreme Lord is indeed *akarma* (non-action) because, as a cause of knowledge, it lacks the quality of being a bond.

However, in the state of one who has ascended (*āruḍha*), even natural action is merely *karma* because it is sublated by the knowledge of the Self as a non-agent. Therefore, the dissolution of action, which was stated in the verse "he who sees non-action in action," has been fully explained.
Now, for one who perceives Brahman alone as the thread woven through the action and its constituent parts, he describes the dissolution of action with the words "Brahman-offering" (*brahmārpaṇam*).
That by which something is offered is the "offering" (*arpaṇa*), such as the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and so forth;
that too is Brahman alone.
Even the oblation being offered, such as clarified butter and the like, is Brahman alone;
the fire is also Brahman alone;
and the act of offering (homa) is that which is poured into that [fire] by Brahman as the agent.
The meaning is that fire, the agent, and the action are all Brahman alone.

Thus, by one whose concentration—meaning one-pointedness of mind—is fixed upon Brahman itself, which consists of action, Brahman alone is to be reached or attained; the meaning is that no other fruit is to be obtained. //24//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might ask: why does an action being performed perish even without producing its fruit? [The Lord] says, "The offering is Brahman," because the cause of that [action] is destroyed through the realization of Brahman.
For an action such as a sacrifice is accomplished by means of numerous causal factors (*kāraka*).

For sacrifice (yāga) is the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity; that very act is called an oblation (homa) because of the casting of the substance being relinquished into the fire. In that context, the deity intended is the recipient (sampradāna).
The substance being abandoned, denoted by the word *havis* (oblation), is the direct object (*karman*) of the root-meaning;
however, its result, such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, is the mediated object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Thus, the ladle (*juhū*) and other implements are the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the most effective means for casting the oblation into the fire through their capacity to sustain it, while mantras and the like are also instruments by virtue of their capacity to manifest [the rite]; thus, the instrument is twofold, distinguished as the actual performer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Thus, there are two actions: relinquishment and casting into the fire.
In the former, the sacrificer is the agent;
in the casting, however, the officiating priest (adhvaryu) hired by the sacrificer is the agent, and the fire is the locus of the casting.
In this way, location, time, and so forth, as well as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), should be understood as common to all actions.

Thus, all conventional transactions involving actions, their factors (*kāraka*s), and so on— which are imagined through the ignorance of Brahman, just like [the snake] imagined through the ignorance of the rope— [are to be understood].

This verse establishes that when the snake, the stream, the staff, and so forth are sublated by the knowledge of the reality of the rope— just as they are by the knowledge of the reality of Brahman— the appearance of the conventional usage of actions, agents, and the like, though still perceived through the persistence of what has been sublated, is no longer capable of producing results, according to the analogy of a burnt cloth.
Furthermore, the vision of Brahman alone is praised as being the essence of all sacrifices.

For instance: by the etymological derivation "that by which something is offered" (*arpyate 'nena*), the instrument (*karaṇa*)—such as the *juhū* ladle and the sacred mantras—is called "offering" (*arpaṇa*).
Likewise, by the etymological derivation "that to which something is offered" (*arpyate 'smai*), the recipient (*sampradāna*) in the form of the deity is called "offering."
By the etymological derivation "that which is offered (*arpyate*) in this," *arpaṇa* refers to the locus, such as place, time, and so forth.
Since all that is imagined within Brahman, it is Brahman alone; the meaning is that, like a snake imagined upon a rope, it is non-existent apart from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Likewise, with respect to the actions of offering the oblation and casting it [into the fire], the direct object (*karman*)—the instrument (*kāraka*)—is also Brahman alone.

Thus, that into which it is cast into the fire is also Brahman alone; "in the fire of Brahman" (*brahmāgnau*) is a compound word. Likewise, both that by which it is abandoned—that is, cast—by the agent, namely the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest, and that very agent-instrument (*kartṛ-kāraka*), having been restated by means of the instrumental case ending prescribed for the agent, is established as being Brahman.
Regarding the word "by Brahman":

thus, that which is offered—that is, the act of offering (*havana*) consisting of both the action of relinquishment and the action of casting [the oblation]—that too is Brahman alone. Likewise, that by which one is to go through the offering—the mediated result such as heaven and so forth—that too is Brahman alone.
The word "eva" (only) occurring here is connected with every instance;
even in the phrase "it has been offered," the word "Brahman" is supplied from this very context.

Because there is no intervention and because of the requirement for syntactic expectancy— as in the case of the supplementary words "with the flawless [mind]" (*acchidreṇa*) and so forth in the passage "May the Lord of Consciousness purify you" (*cit-patiḥ tvā punātu*)—

it follows that by this form [of yoga], even one who is a performer of ritual action (*karman*) but possesses meditative absorption in action (*karma-samādhi*), that is, the knowledge of Brahman, must reach Brahman, which is non-dual supreme bliss. This is what is supplied as the ellipsis.

Because of the expectancy [of the sentence] and the lack of intervention, [the phrase] "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the dust" (*yā te agne rajāśayā*) and so forth is like the completion of the preceding sentence beginning with "the most excellent body" (*tanūr varṣiṣṭhā*).
Alternatively, by the etymology "that which is offered to this [person] as a fruit," the word *arpaṇa* itself includes fruits such as heaven;
thus, the second half of the verse, "Brahman alone is to be reached by him whose work is absorbed in Brahman," is rightly understood as being solely for the purpose of stating the fruit of knowledge.

In this view, "brahma-karma-samādhinā" may be taken as a single compound word; alternatively, it may be taken as two separate words, where the first term "brahma" is connected with the preceding word "hutam," and the last term is connected with the word "gantavya. In this way, one should understand that there is no difficulty regarding the necessity of supplying missing words (anuṣaṅga) twice.
"Brahman is to be reached" means that its attainment occurs precisely through non-difference, used figuratively.

For this very reason, heaven and such inferior fruits are not to be reached by that [knowledge], because through knowledge there is the cessation of the conventional usage of causal agents produced by ignorance.
This has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika:
"For in the conventional usage of causal factors (*kāraka*), a pure reality is not perceived; and if a pure reality were established, from where could there be the exclusion of causal factors?

Thus, without subverting the very nature of the causal factors such as the act of offering (*arpaṇa*) and so forth, the vision of Brahman is projected upon them merely by way of identification, just as [the vision of] a name and so on [is projected].

The commentary of some, which interprets [the passage] as being "for the sake of a specific fruit," has been refuted by the authors of the Bhāṣya themselves through such arguments as its contradiction with the opening statement (*upakrama*) and so forth, and because the mere performance of the ritual (*sampan-mātra*) is not applicable in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*). //24//
Viśvanātha:
It has been stated that one should perform for the sake of sacrifice.
Of what nature is that very sacrifice?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "Brahman.
That by which something is offered is the "offering" (arpaṇa), such as the ladle and so forth;
that too is Brahman alone.
Even the oblation being offered is Brahman alone;
since "Brahman alone [is offered] in Brahman," the fire, which is the locus of the offering, is also Brahman alone.
Thus, by a person possessing such discrimination, Brahman alone is to be reached.
But there is no other fruit.
Why? Because it belongs to one for whom the action is essentially Brahman and who possesses *samādhi*, that is, one-pointedness of mind, directed toward that very [Brahman]. //24//

Baladeva: Having thus described how one's own prescribed action takes the form of knowledge by being imbued with the contemplation of the distinct individual self (*jīvātman*), he now states that it takes that same form through the contemplation of its identity with the Supreme Self (*parātman*) when accompanied by its constituent parts, in the verse beginning "brahmārpaṇam.

Based on the etymology "that by which the Self itself is offered," the *arpaṇa* (the vessel) is the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), as well as the deities presiding over the mantras such as Indra; and all those are indeed Brahman alone.
Even the oblation being offered, such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, is Brahman alone.
And that oblation is offered, relinquished, and cast into the fire—the substratum of the *homa*—which is itself Brahman, by the sacrificer, the *adhvaryu*, and the *brahmā*.
The meaning is that the fire, the sacrificer, and the *adhvaryu* are all Brahman alone.
In the expression "brahmāgnau," the elision of the suffix *ṇi* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage.

Nor should it be said that this is a compound word (*samasta-pada*), because the perception of Brahman within the fire is what is to be enjoined. And thus, there is meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—that is, one-pointedness of mind—upon the ritual action together with its constituent parts, which has the nature of Brahman.
The meaning is that by that seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), Brahman alone is to be reached— that is, its own true nature and the supreme nature are to be attained and beheld.
In passages such as "If one knows Brahman as consciousness," the word *brahman* refers to the individual soul (jīva).
In passages such as "Consciousness, bliss, Brahman," since the Supreme Self is associated with qualities such as being the offering of Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), there is no redundancy in this section.
Commentators explain that the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and other implements are Brahman because their functioning is dependent upon Him and because they are to be attained through Him.
When contemplated in such a manner, action takes on the form of knowledge and is rendered fit for His vision. //24//
Some yogis offer sacrifice solely to the divine; others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman. 4.25

Śrīdhara: This very knowledge, characterized by the perception of Brahman everywhere—which has been accomplished as a sacrifice—is the most excellent of all sacrifices because it is attainable through the means of all sacrifices. To praise it in this way, [the Lord] speaks of the many sacrifices that serve as the means to knowledge, according to the distinctions among qualified aspirants, in the eight verses beginning with "The sacrifice to the gods... and so forth.
In that sacrifice, the gods beginning with Indra and Varuṇa are worshipped;
by the use of the word "eva" (only), it is shown that there is an absence of the realization of Brahman regarding Indra and the others.
Other Karma-yogins attend to that very same divine sacrifice; they perform it with faith.

Others, however, who are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge, offer sacrifice into the fire whose nature is Brahman by means of sacrifice itself—in the manner previously described, such as "the offering is Brahman" and so forth.
The meaning is that they dissolve all actions, beginning with sacrifice, into that fire;
this is the sacrifice of knowledge. //25//

Madhusūdana: Now, since the mantra beginning with "brahmārpaṇam" exists as a praise of right vision by way of its being a sacrifice, [the Lord] again introduces other types of sacrifices for the purpose of praising that [right vision], beginning with the word "daivam."

That by which the gods, such as Indra, Agni, and others, are worshipped is the "divine" (daiva); other yogis constantly perform and attend to that very sacrifice in the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth.

Having thus described the sacrifice of action, [the Lord] now speaks of the sacrifice of knowledge—which results from it—by means of the purification of the internal organ: "In the fire of Brahman. Brahman is the referent of the word *tat* (That), whose nature is truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss, and from whom all distinctions have been eliminated.
In that fire, one should offer the sacrifice—the inner self, the referent of the word "thou" (tvam)—by means of the sacrifice itself;
for Yāska has listed the word "sacrifice" among the names of the Self.
The instrumental case here is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*itthambhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
The particle *eva* serves to exclude both difference and non-difference.
The meaning is that they offer [the world] solely as non-different from the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*), perceiving it as having that very nature.
Others, who are distinct from the former, are those established in the vision of reality (*tattva*).

The meaning is "for the renunciant" (saṃnyāsin). Having established the realization of the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman as a sacrifice, it is recited among the sacrifices that are its means—beginning with the words "Knowledge-sacrifice is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects"—in order to praise it. //25//
Viśvanātha:
Indeed, there are many other sacrifices as well that exist according to their distinctions; "Listen to them," he says, with eight verses beginning with "The divine sacrifice alone."
That in which the gods, such as Indra, Varuṇa, and others, are worshipped is called *daiva*.
This shows the absence of the realization of Brahman regarding Indra and the other deities.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *sāsya devatā*.
The "yogins" are the karma-yogins;

however, others who are jñāna-yogins offer the individual soul (jīva), which corresponds to the referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-pada), as an oblation into that very Brahman— the Supreme Self— which is the fire, the referent of the word "that" (tat-pada), by means of the sacrifice consisting of the mantra in the form of the syllable Om (praṇava).
This very sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajña) will be praised first.

Here, the two words "yajña" and "yajñena" function as the object and the instrument respectively; through a primary hyperbole (atiśayokti), they denote the pure individual soul (śuddha-jīva) and the syllable Om (praṇava). //25//

Baladeva: Having thus described how action takes the form of knowledge by being permeated with the contemplation of Brahman, he speaks of the divisions of Karma-yoga, beginning with the word "daivam" (divine).
Other yogis worship the divine sacrifice consisting of the adoration of Indra and other deities; they establish their firm resolve (*niṣṭhā*) in that alone.

Others, according to the principle of "offering to Brahman" and so forth, offer the sacrifice—which consists of oblations such as clarified butter—into the fire that has become Brahman by means of sacrificial ladles and the like; the meaning is that they establish their firm resolve in the act of oblation itself. //25//
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint; others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses. (4.26)
Śrīdhara: "The ears and so forth.
Others, namely lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins), offer the ears and other senses as oblations into the fires consisting of the restraint of each respective sense-organ;
that is to say, they dissolve them [into those fires], remaining intent upon restraint by restraining the senses.
The senses themselves are the fires.
Into these, other householders offer sound and the rest.
The meaning is that even at the time of enjoying sense objects, being unattached, they cast sound and the rest—conceived as oblations—into the senses, which have been conceived as fires. //26//

Madhusūdana: Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint; others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses. (26)
Viśvanātha:
Others who are lifelong celibates offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires which are the mind itself when it is restrained. They sacrifice into those fires.
The meaning is that they cause the senses to dissolve into the pure mind.

Others, who are inferior to them, are celibate students (*brahmacārins*); they offer the objects such as sound into the fires of the senses—the senses themselves being the fires—meaning they cause sound and the other objects to dissolve into the senses. //26//

Baladeva: Others—namely, lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*)—offer their ears and other senses into the fires of self-restraint (*saṃyama*), which consist of the restraint of each respective sense; having restrained them, they remain devoted primarily to self-restraint.

Others—namely, householders—offer sounds and other objects into the ears and other senses, which have been conceived as fires; enjoying them without attachment, they cause those senses to be inclined toward that [self-restraint]. //26//
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge. (4.27)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "all [actions]":
others explain that this refers to those established in meditation;
it means the functions of the sensory organs, such as hearing, seeing, and so forth.
The functions of the organs of action— speech, hands, and so forth— are speaking, grasping, and the like;
as are the functions of the ten vital breaths (*prāṇas*),
such as the outward movement of the *prāṇa*.
The function of apāna is downward movement;
that of vyāna is pervasive movement, such as contraction and expansion;
and that of samāna is the equalizing distribution of what has been eaten and drunk.
The upward movement of the *udāna* wind: Nāga is said to be responsible for belching; Kūrma is remembered for opening the eyes;
Kṛkara is to be known as the cause of hunger; and Devadatta is for yawning.
The all-pervading Dhanañjaya does not abandon anyone anywhere, even when they have died.
[From the Gheraṇḍa-saṃhitā 5.64:
"They offer oblations in this very manner.
Self-restraint is one-pointedness of meditation upon the Self."
That itself is yoga;
that itself is the fire.

When that [fire] is kindled—that is, set ablaze—by knowledge whose object is the thing to be meditated upon, one should understand the object of meditation correctly, restrain the mind within it, and bring all those actions to rest; this is the meaning. //27//
Madhusūdana:

Regarding that non-difference [of cause and effect], based on the words concerning "origination" and so forth (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.14), others who know the true meaning of the term *tvaṃ-pada* offer all the senses, their functions—namely hearing, seeing, and all other activities of the senses as well as the activities of the vital breaths—as oblations into the fire of self-restraint and yoga, which is kindled by knowledge. (27)
Viśvanātha:
Others are those who possess knowledge of the pure meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-pada).
All the senses and their functions, such as hearing, seeing, and so forth—[are withdrawn].
The functions of the vital breaths are the ten prāṇas and their respective activities:
the outward movement of prāṇa and the downward leading of apāna.
The function of *samāna* is the equalizing of what has been eaten, drunk, and so forth;
that of *udāna* is leading [the breath] upward;
and that of *vyāna* is leading it in all directions.
Nāga is said to be in vomiting; Kūrma is remembered as being in the opening of the eyes; Kṛkara is to be known as that which produces sneezing; Devadatta is in yawning;
and Dhanañjaya, the all-pervading, never leaves [the body] even when one is dead.
[Thus, according to Gheraṇḍa-saṃhitā 5.64: These are the ten vital breaths and their functions.
Self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is indeed the fire for the purification of the Self, which is the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*); into that they offer oblations.

The meaning is that they dissolve the faculties such as the mind and intellect, as well as the ten vital breaths; they contemplate that only the inner self (pratyagātman) alone exists, and nothing else, including the mind and so forth. //27//
Baladeva: "All" refers to the actions of the senses and the actions of the vital breaths. Others offer these into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint (*ātma-saṃyama-yoga*).
Self-restraint of the mind is itself yoga; they offer [the senses and breaths] into that which has been conceived as fire.
Through the mind (*manas*), they strive to restrain the tendency of the sense organs (*indriya*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) toward activity.

The activities of the sense organs, such as hearing and so forth, and the activities of the vital breaths— namely, the outward movement of *prāṇa*, the downward movement of *apāna*, and so on— are [thus restrained].

The pervasion of the entire body by vyāna, the contraction and expansion [of the limbs] and so forth; the equalizing of what is eaten, drunk, and so on by samāna; and the upward leading by udāna—all these are to be understood collectively as being illuminated by knowledge and made radiant by the contemplation of the Self. //27//

Others perform sacrifices with material objects, sacrifices of austerity, and sacrifices of yoga; and others, ascetics of firm vows, perform sacrifices of self-study and sacrifices of knowledge. (4.28)
Śrīdhara: "Those whose sacrifice is material substance" (dravya-yajña), and so forth.
Those for whom the giving of material substance itself is the sacrifice are "sacrificers of material substance.
Those for whom austerity such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances is the sacrifice are "sacrificers of austerity."
Those for whom yoga itself, consisting of its eight limbs, is the sacrifice are the "sacrificers of yoga" (yoga-yajñāḥ).

Those for whom the knowledge of the meaning derived from self-study—that is, from the Veda through hearing, reflection, and so forth—is itself the sacrifice are the "sacrificers of self-study and knowledge" (svādhyāya-jñāna-yajñāḥ).
Alternatively, they are of two kinds: those who offer the sacrifice of reciting the Vedas and those who offer the sacrifice of knowing their meaning.
The *yatayas* are those habituated to effort;
they are those whose vows (*vrata*) have been properly sharpened—that is, made keen. //28//
Madhusūdana:

Others, however, are performers of sacrifice through material objects, sacrifice through austerity, and sacrifice through yoga; likewise, there are ascetics of firm vows who perform sacrifice through Vedic study and sacrifice through knowledge. (28)
Viśvanātha:
Those for whom the sacrifice consists solely of the giving of material goods are "sacrificers of material goods" (dravya-yajña).
Those for whom the sacrifice consists solely of austerity, such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, are "sacrificers of austerity" (tapa-yajña).

Those for whom yoga is indeed the eightfold sacrifice are the "sacrificers of yoga" (yoga-yajña). Those for whom self-study—both the recitation of the Veda and the knowledge of its meaning—is the sacrifice are the [sacrificers of study].
The "strivers" (yatayaḥ) are those intent on effort.
All these are those whose vows have been perfectly cooled and sharpened. //28//
Baladeva: Regarding the word "dravya" (substance):
some karma-yogins are performers of sacrifices of substance, devoted to the giving of food and so forth;
others are performers of sacrifices of austerity, devoted to vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*.

Some are performers of the sacrifice of study and knowledge, devoted to the recitation of the Vedas and devoted to the study of their meaning; they are ascetics habitually diligent in that regard, firm in their vows, and strict in their respective practices. //28//
Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna and likewise the apāna into the prāṇa;
having restrained the movements of both prāṇa and apāna, they are devoted to prāṇāyāma. (4.29)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the apāna":
when the apāna moves downward, they offer the upward-moving prāṇa into it by means of pūraka;
at the time of pūraka, they unify the prāṇa with the apāna.
Likewise, having restrained the upward and downward movements of the prāṇa and apāna by means of retention (kumbhaka), they offer the apāna into the prāṇa at the time of exhalation (recaka).
Thus, the meaning is that "others" are those devoted to prāṇāyāma through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
Furthermore, as for the term "others": [it refers to those who practice in this manner].
Others, however, practicing the restriction of food, meditate upon the dissolution of the respective functions of the senses as the senses themselves naturally decay; this is the meaning.

Or else, by the statement "some offer the prāṇa into the apāna, and likewise others the apāna into the prāṇa," [it refers to] the oneness of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* through the *ajāpā-mantra*—which is manifested as "haṃsaḥ so 'ham" (I am He) in both forward and reverse order—as the inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*) revolve.
The meaning is that they cultivate [the practice] through mutual exchange.
As it is said in the Yoga-śāstra:
"With the sound *sa*, one goes out; with the sound *haṃ*, one enters again."
"One should contemplate: 'The vital breath (prāṇa) therein is that very I, the Haṃsa.
By this verse beginning with "having restrained the movements of prāṇa and apāna," the sacrifices of breath-control (prāṇāyāma-yajña) are described by others.
In this regard, the meaning is as follows: one should fill two parts with food and fill one part with water.
"One should leave a fourth part for the sake of movement"—
those whose food is restricted according to such scriptural injunctions,
having blocked the flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths by means of *kumbhaka*, being devoted to *prāṇāyāma*, offer the vital breaths (the senses) into the vital breaths.

For in *kumbhaka* (retention), all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) become unified; thus, the meaning is that one should contemplate the *homa* (sacrificial oblation) while the senses are being dissolved right there.
As it is said in the *Yoga-śāstra*:
"In whatever way, through constant practice, stability of the mind may arise..."
And likewise, there is stability of the winds, speech, body, and views, in that very manner. //29//
Madhusūdana: Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna and the apāna into the prāṇa; having restrained the movements of both prāṇa and apāna, they are devoted to prāṇāyāma. (29)
Viśvanātha:
Others, devoted to prāṇāyāma, offer the upward-moving prāṇa into the downward-moving apāna during the time of inhalation (pūraka), thereby unifying prāṇa with apāna;
likewise, during the time of exhalation (recaka), they offer the apāna into the prāṇa.
At the time of *kumbhaka*, having restrained the movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, they become devoted to *prāṇāyāma*;

others, desiring mastery over the senses, maintain restricted diets or eat very little; and as the vital breaths continue to live through the very reduction of food, they offer their senses into those breaths as an oblation.

Since the functioning of the sense organs is dependent upon the vital breath (prāṇa), when the vital breath becomes weak, the sense organs themselves become incapable of grasping their respective objects; thus, they dissolve back into the vital breaths—this is the meaning. //29//
Baladeva: "And what about 'in the apāna'? Others, devoted to prāṇāyāma, perform it in three ways: they offer the upward-moving prāṇa into the downward-moving apāna;
by means of inhalation (pūraka), they unify the prāṇa with the apāna.
Likewise, they offer the apāna into the prāṇa; by means of exhalation (recaka), having unified the apāna with the prāṇa, they cause it to go out.
Just as the movements of prāṇa and apāna—namely inhalation and exhalation—are restrained through retention (kumbhaka), so they proceed.
The outward exit of the internal air through the nose and mouth is inhalation, which is the movement of the prāṇa.
The entry of that [air] which has gone out is exhalation (*praśvāsa*), the movement of the *apāna*.
The restraint of these two is *kumbhaka*; it is of two kinds: internal *kumbhaka* is the restraint of inhalation and exhalation after filling the air;
external *kumbhaka* is the restraint of those two after expelling the air.

Others, subsisting on the food of eternalism, practice the restriction of eating and offer the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the senses into the breaths. As these [breaths] waste away due to scant food, the senses—which have their functions dependent upon them—become incapable of perceiving objects and dissolve right there, like drops of water poured onto a heated iron plate. //29//
Others, with their food restricted, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose sins have been destroyed by sacrifice.

Śrīdhara: Thus, he states the fruit for these twelve types of performers of sacrifice who have been mentioned, beginning with "All these... Those who find or obtain sacrifices are called *yajña-vidaḥ*, or alternatively, those who know sacrifices (*yajña-jñāḥ*).
Those by whom the impurity has been exhausted—that is, destroyed—by means of sacrifices. //30//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, he states the fruit for those who know the twelve kinds of sacrifice mentioned above with the words "All these...
Those who know the sacrifices (*yajña-vidaḥ*) are those who know, understand, or obtain the sacrifices; that is, the knowers and performers of sacrifices.
Those whose sins and impurities have been destroyed or eliminated by the sacrifices previously mentioned are "those whose impurities are destroyed by sacrifice" (*yajña-kṣapita-kalmaṣāḥ*).

Having performed sacrifices, they eat food—designated by the word *amṛta* (nectar)—during the time remaining after [the sacrificial duties]; thus they are "those who eat the nectar remaining from sacrifice" (*yajña-śiṣṭāmṛta-bhujaḥ*).
All of them, by means of the purification of the mind and the attainment of knowledge, go to the eternal Brahman; the meaning is that they are liberated from saṃsāra. //30//
Viśvanātha:
All these [practitioners], being knowers of sacrifice (yajña-vidas)—meaning those who find the sacrifices characterized as previously described—attain Brahman by means of knowledge.

Here, he states the result not previously mentioned: they enjoy that which is the remnant of sacrifice (yajña-śiṣṭa), the residue of sacrifice, namely the nectar consisting of enjoyment, sovereignty, supernatural powers (siddhi), and so forth. //30//
Baladeva said: "Indeed, all these people desire victory over the senses; so say those who know sacrifice.
Finding fulfillment through the previously mentioned sacrifices to the gods and others, their impurities are destroyed by those very sacrifices. (30)
Those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman.
This world is not for one who does not sacrifice; how then could there be another, O best of the Kurus? (4.31)
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice":

having performed sacrifices, they eat at the remaining time food that is not forbidden and which is of the nature of nectar; thus it is so described. They attain the eternal, perpetual Brahman by means of knowledge.
He states the fault in not performing that [sacrifice] with the words "not this":

even this human world, though it possesses little happiness, does not belong to one who has not performed sacrifice—that is, one who is devoid of the performance of sacrifice. How much less so the other world, which possesses great happiness?
Therefore, the meaning is that sacrifices must be performed in every way. //31//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus stated the excellence in the case of conformity, he declares the defect in the case of deviation with the half-verse beginning with "ye yajñāḥ. Among the sacrifices mentioned, he who lacks even one of them is "ayajña"; for such a person, even this human world of meager pleasure does not exist, because he is censured by all.
O best of the Kurus, how could there be another world to be accomplished through any other distinguished means? //31//
Viśvanātha:
He states the fruit thus intended with the words "they go to Brahman. He states the transgression incurred by not performing it with the words "not this."
This human world, which possesses but little happiness, does not even exist; how much less so any other world, such as that of the gods, which could be attained by him—this is the meaning. //31//
Baladeva: He states the unintended fruit with the words "yajña-śiṣṭa" (the remnant of sacrifice).
This refers to those who enjoy the remnant of sacrifice, which is the nectar-like food and so forth, as well as the attainment of enjoyments, sovereignty, perfections, and the like.
He states the intended fruit with the word "yānti" (they go).
"Brahman" [is understood] by means of the knowledge to be accomplished by that [means], as previously stated. //30//
Thus, many kinds of sacrifices are spread out in the mouth of Brahman; know them all to be born of action, and by knowing this, you shall be liberated. 32.

Śrīdhara: In order to praise the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñāna-yajña*), he concludes the sacrifices previously mentioned with the words "thus manifold" (*evaṃ bahu-vidhā*). They are "spread at the mouth of Brahman," meaning they are directly enjoined by the Veda.

Nevertheless, know—that is, understand—all those [actions] born of speech, mind, and body to be devoid of contact with the true nature of the Self, because the Self is not within the sphere of action. Having known this and being established in knowledge, you shall be liberated from saṃsāra. //32//
Madhusūdana:
Is this being said by you merely on the basis of your own imagination? For is it not the case that the Veda alone is the authority here? To this he says, "Thus" (evam).

Thus, as described, the various kinds of sacrifices—of many types and forms, consisting of the means for attaining all Vedic welfare—are spread out; they are extended at the mouth, that is, the door, of the Brahman, which is the Veda; indeed, these [sacrifices] are accessible only through the door of the Veda.
The meaning is that they have been understood.
As for the Vedic sentences, however, they are not cited individually here for fear of prolixity.
Know—that is, understand—all those sacrifices to be born of action (*karmaja*), arising from physical, vocal, and mental acts; do not consider them to be born of the Self.

For the Self is indeed devoid of activity; these [states] are not its activities. Rather, by knowing "I am inactive and indifferent," you will be liberated from this bondage of saṃsāra—this is the remainder [of the sense]. //32//
Viśvanātha:
The meaning is that they were clearly spoken by the mouth of Brahmā—that is, by the Veda, which is his own mouth. "Born of action" means produced by the actions of speech, mind, and body. //32//
Baladeva: "So it is.
They are spread across the mouth of Brahmā—that is, the Veda;
they have been clearly uttered by him himself as the means for attaining the distinct Self.
"Born of karma" means produced by the actions of speech, mind, and body.

Having understood this, and having realized those [teachings] taught as the means thereto and practiced them, you will be liberated from saṃsāra once you have perceived the two types of self through the wisdom arising therefrom. //32//
O scorcher of foes, a sacrifice of knowledge is superior to a sacrifice performed with material objects.
O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge. (4.33)
Śrīdhara: He says "superior" (*śreyān*) to show that the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñāna-yajña*) is indeed superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (*karma-yajña*).

The sacrifice of knowledge is superior—that is, more excellent—than the sacrifice consisting of material substances (*dravya-maya*), which is produced by the activity of the non-self (the body) such as sacrifices to the gods and so forth.

Although the sacrifice of knowledge is likewise dependent upon the activity of the mind, nevertheless, knowledge, which is the very nature of the Self, is merely manifested within a modification of the mind.
It is not the state of being produced from that [knowledge] which constitutes the distinction from that which consists of material substance.
The reason for its superiority is as follows: "All action in its entirety, together with its fruit, culminates in knowledge";
the meaning is that it becomes included within it.
"He fully comprehends all that which people do well," according to the Śruti. //33//
Madhusūdana:
