Since all [paths] have been mentioned as equal, and thus an equivalence between action and knowledge might be inferred, he says "superior" (śreyān).
It is superior—that is, more praiseworthy—because its fruit is liberation directly.

Compared to every other sacrifice— even one consisting of material objects, characterized by such things, and devoid of knowledge, which yields the fruit of saṃsāra— the sacrifice of knowledge alone is superior,
O scorcher of foes!
Why is this so?

Because all action—whether Vedic in its entirety and without exception, consisting of the *iṣṭi*, animal sacrifice, *soma* sacrifice, and fire-altar construction (*cayana*), or Smārta in the form of meditations and so forth—is completed in the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self; that is, it culminates through the removal of obstacles.
This is according to the Śruti: "Brahmins seek to know this [Self] by means of Vedic recitation, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting," and "By means of dharma, one casts off evil."

The meaning is that this is also because of the principle stated in the sūtra: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (VS 3.4.26). //33//
Viśvanātha:

Among those, even compared to the sacrifice consisting of material substances—which is characterized by the verse beginning "The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman"—the sacrifice of knowledge mentioned by the words "in the fire of Brahman" is superior.
Why? Because when knowledge exists, all action in its entirety becomes non-futile and reaches completion; that is, it attains its final fulfillment.
The meaning is that after knowledge, karma does not persist. //33//

Baladeva: The modes of action (*karma-yoga*) have been described as being like a forest, because they contain within them the contemplation of the isolated Self (*viviktātman*), and thus possess a dual nature. Among these, he praises the aspect consisting of knowledge with the words "the better" (*śreyān*).

Within the two-fold form of action, the part consisting of knowledge is "better"—that is, more praiseworthy—than the part consisting of material action, due to the fear [of bondage] inherent in material action.

The phrase "than that consisting of material substance" (*dravya-mayāt*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the control of the senses and so forth, since those are the means to that [knowledge].

He explains this: O Pārtha, when knowledge exists, all action in its entirety—including its constituent parts—is completely brought to an end and ceases; for it is observed that once the result has been produced, the means of attainment cease. //33//
Learn that by humble prostration, by inquiry, and by service; the wise who have seen the truth will instruct you in that knowledge. (4.34)
Śrīdhara: He states the means for such knowledge of the Self with the word "that.
"That" refers to that knowledge; the meaning is: know it, understand it, and attain it—by prostration, that is, by bowing down like a staff, to those who possess knowledge.
Then, through inquiry:
"From where does this saṃsāra of mine arise? Or how might it cease?"
Thus, by means of inquiry,
by service, and by attendance upon the teacher,
one approaches those who possess knowledge— that is, those learned in the scriptures.
They are seers of reality and endowed with direct experience;
they will provide you with knowledge through instruction. //34//
Madhusūdana:
Regarding the attainment of such knowledge, it is said that the most proximate means is "know that" (*tad viddhi*).
Know—that is, obtain—that knowledge which is the fruit of all actions by approaching the teachers and prostrating before them.

Prostration (*praṇipāta*) is falling down very low; it is a long-lasting salutation. By means of this, one asks many questions concerning various subjects, such as: "Who am I? How am I bound? By what means might I be liberated? and so forth. Service (*sevā*) consists of acting in accordance with [the teacher's] wishes through every aspect of one's being.

Thus, being inclined toward you by virtue of a particular prostration preceded by an excess of devotion and faith, those knowers—who are skilled in the means of knowledge such as words, sentences, and logic; who are seers of reality; and who have attained direct realization—will instruct you and thereby bring about for you that knowledge concerning the Supreme Self which has liberation as its immediate fruit.

The Blessed One’s view is that knowledge imparted by those who possess direct realization alone culminates in its fruit, and not even that which is provided by those devoid of such realization, however skilled they may be in the measurement of words, sentences, and logic. This is in agreement with the Śruti: "To understand that, one should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in hand—a master of the Vedas (śrotriya) who is firmly established in Brahman.
In this context as well, the explanation is that a *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Vedas, and one "established in Brahman" is one who has achieved the direct realization of Brahman.
This plural number refers to the teacher; it is used for the sake of expressing extreme reverence even toward a single person, and not with the intention of denoting multiplicity.
It should be understood that once the knowledge of reality has arisen from a single teacher who has realized that reality, it is improper to go to another teacher for that same purpose. //34//
Viśvanātha:
He states the method for attaining that knowledge with the word "tat" (that). By prostration—that is, by bowing down like a staff—to the guru, the instructor of knowledge.
O Blessed One, from where does this saṃsāra of mine arise?
How will it cease?

Thus, by means of inquiry and by service—that is, by attending upon him—one should approach the teacher for the sake of knowing that [Brahman], with fuel in hand, according to the Śruti: "One should approach a teacher who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman. //34//

Baladeva: Having thus taught the knowledge of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) along with its means and all its auxiliary parts, and now teaching the knowledge of the worship of the Supreme Being, He states that this is obtainable through association with the virtuous (sat), beginning with the words: "That which is the purpose for which both of these have been taught by Me to you—know that to be indestructible" (Gītā 2.17).
You [should obtain] that knowledge concerning the Supreme Self from virtuous knowers who have been propitiated by prostrations and other such means.
"Having realized your own true nature, know [it] and attain it.
In this context, *praṇipāta* is prostration like a staff;
*sevā* is service to them like that of a servant.
"Paripraśnaḥ" refers to various questions concerning His essential nature, His qualities, and His manifestations.
If it be objected that they, being indifferent, will not speak, he says "upetya":
those wise ones, having realized the Self as their own true nature, perceiving your desire to know Him through prostration and other signs, [will speak] to you.
To such a person, those who perceive reality—the compassionate ones who propagate that knowledge—will teach the knowledge concerning Him (the Self).

If it is argued that here the word "that" (*tat*) must refer to the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*), because it is the subject under discussion, we say no; for [the Lord has declared]: "Never was I not" (Gītā 2.12).
"One should sit disciplined, intent on Me" (Gītā 2.61), and "Though unborn, the immutable Self" (Gītā 4.6); because of such passages, the Supreme Self is also non-material (*aprākṛta*).
Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "And the reference is for another purpose" (VS 1.3.20).
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the subsequent greatness of knowledge which accords with the meaning of the Śruti and the Sūtras; thus it has been well stated. //34//
O Pāṇḍava, having known that [knowledge], you will not again fall into such delusion; by means of it, you shall see all beings without exception within yourself, and then within me. (4.35)
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of that knowledge with three and a half verses beginning with "Having known which" (*yaj jñātvā*).
Having known—that is, having attained—this knowledge, you will not again fall into delusion caused by the killing of kinsmen and the like.
The reason for this is: by means of that knowledge, you will see all beings—such as father, son, and so forth, which are the manifestations of your own ignorance—as non-different from your very self.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, you will perceive the Self as non-different from Me, the Supreme Self; this is the meaning. //35//
Madhusūdana:
What would happen if knowledge were produced through such excessive persistence? To this he says, "Having known that" (yaj jñātvā).
Having known—that is, having attained—the aforementioned knowledge taught by the teachers.
Just as in the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odana-pākaṃ pacati*),
there is the use of that very same verbal root with the intention of expressing a general sense;
you shall not, however, fall into such delusion caused by the slaughter of kinsmen and the like.
O scorcher of foes,
why is it so? Because by means of this knowledge, all beings— beginning with fathers and sons and extending without exception from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—
are seen as the manifestations of one's own ignorance, existing within yourself, the referent of the word "thou," and likewise within me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
In that referent of the word "That," which is in reality devoid of difference and serves as the substratum, you shall see [me] only as non-different;
for there is no existence of the imagined apart from the substratum.

The sense is that, having realized me, the Blessed One Vāsudeva, as one's own self, all ignorance will be destroyed, and consequently, the elements which are its effects will no longer persist. //35//
Viśvanātha:
He states the fruit of this knowledge with three and a half verses beginning with "yaj jñātvā.

Having known that very knowledge—namely, the defining characteristic that the Self is indeed transcendent of the body—you shall no longer incur delusion, which is a property of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

And by that removal of delusion, through the attainment of the knowledge of the Self as eternally established in its own nature, you will see all beings—humans, animals, and so forth—who exist as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within the Self, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), as distinct [from it];
furthermore, you will see them as existing as effects within Me, the supreme cause. //35//
Baladeva: He states the fruit of the aforementioned knowledge with the words "that which" (yat).

Having known—that is, having attained—that knowledge concerning the Supreme Self preceded by the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva), you will no longer fall into such delusion caused by the killing of kinsmen and so forth.
To the question "How shall I not fall [into it]?", he says "by which" (yena).
By that knowledge, you will see all beings—the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth—without exception, meaning in their entirety;
you will see them as existing as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within the Self, which is your own true nature, as something distinct.
Furthermore, you will see them as existing as effects within Me, the Lord of all and the cause of all.

This is what is meant: the individual souls (jīvātmanas), though distinct from the two bodies, have—by the very māyā of Hari—been made to conceive of "mineness" regarding those bodies and their bodily functions, since they are turned away from Hari.
Furthermore, the appearance of the relationship between the slayer and the slain is also produced by that same [māyā];
for those whose true nature is pure, no such connection exists.

Indeed, the Supreme Self, the Lord of all, provides for the individual souls who depend upon Him their respective bodies, senses, the maintenance of those bodies, and the enjoyment of various pleasures in other worlds, in accordance with their respective karmas; yet, when He is worshipped, He grants liberation—thus, for the man of knowledge, there is no room for delusion. //35//
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone. (4.36)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the words "even if" (*api cet*):

even if you are a greater sinner than all other evildoers, nevertheless, you shall cross the entire ocean of sin by means of the raft of knowledge—that is, by the boat of knowledge alone—easily and without effort. (36)
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, listen to the majesty of knowledge [as expressed in the words] "api ced" (even if).
The two particles "api" and "ced" are used for the purpose of indicating the acceptance of what is otherwise considered impossible.
Even though this meaning is indeed impossible,
it is nevertheless stated provisionally for the sake of describing the fruit of knowledge.
Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, the supreme doer of evil;
Nevertheless, all evil—sin, which is like an ocean due to its extreme difficulty of crossing—shall be crossed over by means of the raft of knowledge alone, and not by any other;
having made knowledge itself the raft or boat, you will cross it completely, without effort, and with the state of being free from rebirth. You shall transcend it.

By the word *vṛjina* (sin/obstacle), what is intended here is action (*karman*) in the form of both dharma and adharma, which results in saṃsāra; for one who desires liberation, even merit is undesirable, just like evil. //36//
Viśvanātha:
He speaks of the majesty of knowledge with the words "api cet" (even if).
Even if you are a greater evildoer than even those who are sinful—that is, than those who commit evil deeds—[you shall attain liberation].
Nevertheless, if there is such a degree of sin here, how can there be purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)?
And in its absence, how can the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*) occur?

Furthermore, such wicked conduct could not possibly exist for one in whom knowledge has already arisen. Therefore, the following is the explanation of the venerable Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī: the words "api cet" (even if) are intended to demonstrate the acceptance of what is otherwise considered impossible.
These are particles (*nipāta*).
Although this meaning is indeed impossible, it is stated as a concession for the sake of describing the fruit of knowledge; such is the point. //36//
Baladeva: With the words "Even if" (*api cet*), he speaks of the power of knowledge.

Even though you may be a greater sinner than all other evildoers, nevertheless, you shall cross over all evil—every sin, which is like an ocean because it is difficult to traverse—by means of the boat of knowledge characterized as previously described. //36//
Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. (4.37)
Śrīdhara: [The opponent] might have the misconception that for one who remains like the ocean, there is merely the crossing over of sin, but not the destruction of sin;
warding off this error by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as dry wood... and so forth.

Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel and wood to ashes, so the seeker of liberation who has attained self-knowledge finds and obtains [the Self] within the Self after a long time; this is the meaning. //37//
Madhusūdana:
Now, raising the objection that there might not be a destruction of actions through crossing over [the ocean] of karma as there is in the case of the sea, he states another illustration: "Just as...
fire. Just as a well-kindled, blazing fire reduces pieces of wood—that is, logs—to ashes, bringing them to the state of being ash.

O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions—both sins and merits—without distinction, except for those whose fruits have already begun to manifest, to ashes; that is to say, it destroys them by annihilating the ignorance that is their cause.
And so says the Śruti:
"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,

and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8). Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging of future karma and the destruction of past karma, because of the scriptural declaration thereof.

Regarding the other [karmas] as well, there is no connection [to future births], according to the sūtra: "But at death [the rest perishes]" (4.1.14). As for the fact that merit and demerit that have not yet begun to bear fruit are simply destroyed, the sūtra on this point is: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun perish, until the limit [of that body]" (4.1.15). However, those karmas that initiated the body which produced knowledge perish only at the end of that very body.

This is because of the Śruti text: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), and because of the Sūtra: "But having exhausted the others through experience, he attains [the Supreme]" (Brahma Sūtra 4.1.19).
However, for those who hold offices of authority, the very same bodies that initiated their knowledge are also the ones that initiate their subsequent bodies.
As in the case of Vasiṣṭha, Apāntaratamas, and others;
and likewise the Sūtra states: "The persistence of those entrusted with a specific office lasts as long as their office" (Sūtra 3.3.32).
Here, "office" (adhikāra) refers to powerful karma that has begun to bear fruit and which initiates multiple bodies.
And that [merit] belongs only to lay followers (*upāsaka*), not to others.
Those whose fruits have not yet begun perish; however, those whose fruits have already begun remain until the completion of their enjoyment.
Furthermore, there is no distinction as to whether enjoyment occurs with a single body or with many; however, the detailed account should be consulted in the original source. //37//
Viśvanātha:

[The Lord] says "yathā" (just as) with an illustration, explaining that for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified, [the fire of knowledge] destroys only those karmas other than *prārabdha* (commenced karma) once it has arisen.
"Samiddhaḥ" means fully ignited. //37//
Baladeva: It has been stated that sinful actions are destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman;
now he says "just as" (yathā) to show that meritorious actions are also destroyed.
Just as a well-kindled, blazing fire reduces pieces of wood to ashes, [so does knowledge consume all karma].

Likewise, the fire of knowledge—the flame of the experience of one's own and the Supreme Self—reduces all karmas, both meritorious and sinful, other than those already set in motion (*prārabdha*), to ashes.

Among these, it burns away the accumulated karmas (*sañcita*) that are not yet operative, like a tuft of cotton; it renders the currently being performed (*kriyamāṇa*) karmas as ineffective as a drop of water on a lotus leaf;
but as for the *prārabdha* karmas, even though they are worn out by its power, they persist for the sake of proceeding upon the path of the righteous by the grace of Hari.
"He establishes himself in a state experienced by his own will.
And the Śruti says: "He, being immortal, indeed crosses over both these—the good and the evil.

The meaning is that this experiencer of Brahman, having reflected upon both these—these good and evil actions consisting of merit and demerit being performed—crosses over them, that is, transcends them.

Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-attachment and destruction of the subsequent and prior parts [of karma], because of the designation thereof," and so forth (VS 4.1.13). //37//
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time. 38.
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this with the words "for not," etc.
"Purifying" means that which effects purification.
Among these—tapas, yoga, and so forth—there is indeed nothing equal to knowledge.
If that is so, why do not all people practice the knowledge of the Self alone?
To this he says, in the verse consisting of one and a half lines: "That [knowledge], by itself.
That knowledge regarding the Self, once one has become perfected—that is, attained fitness—through the yoga of action over a long period of time, one obtains by oneself, without effort.
But the meaning is that it is not [attained] without karma-yoga. //38//
Madhusūdana: Because it is so, therefore [the Lord says] "not indeed" (*na hi*).
Indeed, there exists nothing else in this world—whether in the Veda or in worldly affairs—that is as purifying, sanctifying, or cleansing as knowledge.

Because that which is distinct from knowledge does not remove ignorance, it lacks the capacity to eradicate sin along with its root; furthermore, since the causal conditions remain present, sin arises once again.

However, through knowledge, by means of the removal of ignorance, sin is eradicated along with its root. Since nothing else exists that is equal to this, why does that knowledge whose object is the Self not arise immediately for everyone?

Regarding that, he says: "That knowledge, perfected by yoga"—meaning one who has been perfected, refined, and attained fitness through the previously mentioned *karma-yoga*—finds and obtains it within himself, in his own internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*).

The meaning is that one who has attained fitness through yoga does not find it as something given by another and made his own by depending on himself, nor does he find it as something belonging to another and made his own by depending on that other. //38//
Viśvanātha:
Among those engaged in austerity, yoga, and the like, there is nothing whatsoever that is as purifying as knowledge;
yet that knowledge is not easily accessible to all.
But he who is truly perfected through yoga— that is, through the yoga of action performed without desire—
and not one who is unripened, even he [attains this] only in due time.
But it is not immediate;
he finds what has been attained within himself by his own effort.
The sense is that it does not occur merely by the act of taking up renunciation. //38//
Baladeva says: "No, indeed.
For there is no austerity—such as wandering to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth—that is as purifying or cleansing as knowledge;
therefore, that knowledge which destroys all sins is not easily accessible to everyone.
But one who has attained perfection through yoga— that is, through desireless action— finds it within himself by time alone,
not immediately.
He finds that which was already obtained within his own self.
But it is not by the mere act of taking up the life of a wandering mendicant. //38//
The one possessed of faith, intent upon that, and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay. (4.39)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "possessing faith" (śraddhāvān) means one who has a conviction of truth regarding the matter taught by the guru; "devoted to that" (tatparaḥ) means one whose sole focus is that.
And one whose senses are restrained attains that knowledge,
and no other.
Therefore, until the attainment of knowledge through the perfection of faith and other virtues, one must practice Karma-yoga alone for the sake of purification.
But after the attainment of knowledge, there remains nothing further to be done; thus He says: "But having attained knowledge, one attains liberation before long. (39)
Madhusūdana:

That means by which the attainment of knowledge occurs with absolute certainty is said to be more proximate than the previously mentioned prostration and so forth; this is referred to as "possessing faith" (*śraddhāvān*).
Faith is a conviction in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the words of the Guru and the Vedānta, thinking "it is thus and so"; the person who possesses that [faith] obtains knowledge.
Even such a person might be indolent; therefore, he says "intent upon that" (*tat-paraḥ*), meaning one who is intensely devoted to the means of knowledge, such as service to the guru.
Even one who is intent upon that and possesses faith might have uncontrolled senses; therefore, he says "one whose senses are restrained" (*saṃyatendriyaḥ*).
One by whom the senses have been restrained—turned back from their objects—is "one whose senses are restrained.
He who is endowed with these three qualifications necessarily attains knowledge.
However, external acts such as prostration are inconclusive, because they may also arise from deceitfulness and the like.
The meaning is that possessing faith and so forth is the unerring means.

Having attained knowledge by such a means, one attains—that is, reaches—the supreme, final peace, which consists in the cessation of ignorance and its effects, liberation, without delay and without any intervening interval.
For just as a lamp brings about the removal of darkness by its mere arising, and does not require any auxiliary cause; so too is this.

In the same way, knowledge also brings about the cessation of ignorance by its mere arising; it does not depend upon anything such as *prasaṅkhyāna* (contemplative meditation). This is the intended meaning. //39//
Viśvanātha:
Then, being of what nature and at what time does one attain [it]? To this he says: "the man of faith" (śraddhāvān).

Faith is the conviction in the meaning of the scriptures—that knowledge arises only through the purification of the internal organ by means of selfless action (*niṣkāma-karman*). One who possesses that is indeed "the man of faith."

When one who is devoted to that [knowledge], intent upon its practice, and even such a person becomes one whose senses are restrained, then he attains supreme peace, which is the destruction of saṃsāra. //39//
Baladeva says: To explain in what state and when one attains [knowledge], he says, "one who possesses faith" (*śraddhāvān*).
Since knowledge arises through the purification of the heart by means of desireless action, "faith" (*śraddhā*) is firm conviction; one who possesses that is "one who possesses faith."
When one is devoted to that, intent on its performance, and likewise has the senses restrained, then one attains supreme peace, which is liberation. //39//
The ignorant man, the faithless man, and the man of a doubting nature perish.
For the man of a doubting nature, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (40)
Śrīdhara: Having described the qualified person for knowledge, he speaks of the unqualified person who is the opposite of that, beginning with "and the ignorant.
The "ignorant" (ajña) is one who does not understand the meaning taught by the guru;
furthermore, even if some knowledge has somehow arisen, he lacks faith in it.
Even when faith has arisen, one whose mind is overcome by doubt—thinking, "Will this be accomplished for me or not?"—is destroyed;
he falls away from his own goal. Among these three types of persons, one who is characterized by doubt is ruined in every way.

For him, this world does not exist because the acquisition of wealth, marriage, and so forth are unaccomplished; nor does the next world exist because righteousness is not perfected; nor is there happiness, since even the enjoyment of pleasures is impossible due to constant doubt. //40//
Madhusūdana: And in this matter, no doubt should be entertained;
why? Because [the opponent] is ignorant.
The ignorant one is devoid of self-knowledge because he has not studied the scriptures.

One who possesses the atheistic intellect—which is a form of misconception consisting of the thought that "the meaning of the words of the Guru and the Vedānta is certainly not thus"—is faithless (*aśraddadhāna*).
One whose mind is everywhere overcome by doubt, thinking "Is this so, or is it not?", is of a doubting nature (*saṃśayātmā*) and perishes; that is, he falls away from his own true purpose.
The use of the two particles *ca* (and) in the phrase "the ignorant and the faithless perish" is intended to indicate their inferiority in comparison to the one whose nature is doubt.

Why? Because the one whose nature is doubt is the most sinful of all; for him, this human world does not exist due to the absence of wealth-accumulation and such, nor does the next world exist due to the absence of knowledge of dharma, such as regarding heaven and liberation.
Happiness produced by food and such things does not belong to one whose nature is characterized by doubt—that is, one whose mind is pervaded by uncertainty everywhere.

Furthermore, for the one who is ignorant and lacks faith, there is no world beyond, nor is there the human world or the happiness of food and so forth; such is the case for the one whose nature is doubt.
The meaning is that, by virtue of being devoid of the triad [of qualities], he is the most wicked of all. //40//
Viśvanātha:
Having described the qualified recipient of knowledge, he speaks of the opposite type of qualified recipient with the words "and the ignorant.
The ignorant one is deluded like a beast and so forth.
One who lacks faith (aśraddadhānaḥ), even though possessing knowledge of the scriptures, sees the mutual contradictions among various disputants and thus has no confidence in anything whatsoever.
Even one who possesses faith (śraddhāvattve 'pi) may be of a doubting nature (saṃśayātmā), his mind overcome by the hesitation, "Will this be accomplished for me or not?
Among these [two types], he specifically censures the one of a doubting nature with the words "not this" (nāyam). //40//
Baladeva: Having described the one qualified for knowledge and its fruit, he now describes the opposite case and its fruit, beginning with "But the ignorant" (*ajñaś ca*).
The "ignorant" (*ajña*) is one devoid of scriptural knowledge, like animals and the like.
The "faithless" (*aśraddadhāna*) is one who, despite possessing scriptural knowledge, has no conviction anywhere due to conflicting opinions.
Even if one possesses faith, one whose mind is characterized by doubt—wondering, "Will this succeed for me or not?"—perishes; he falls away from his own goal.
Among those very people, he censures the doubter, saying, "He is not [one of us].
This world is common, while the other is extraordinary; for the doubting soul, there is not even the slightest happiness.

For happiness is indeed produced by action prescribed in the scriptures, and that action is preceded by the knowledge of the Self as distinct [from the body]; the meaning is: how can that [happiness] belong to one who is in doubt regarding that [Self]? //40//
O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge, and who possesses self-mastery. 41.

Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "yogena," he concludes the twofold steadfastness in Brahman (*brahma-niṣṭhā*) consisting of action and knowledge, as described in the preceding two chapters through their distinction as prior and subsequent stages.

For one by whom actions have been surrendered to Him through yoga—which consists of the worship of the Supreme Lord—actions do not bind him with their own fruits. Furthermore, for that self-possessed (*ātmavat*) and vigilant person whose worldly cycle—characterized by the false identification with the body and so forth—has been severed by the agent that is the realization of the Self (*ātma-bodha*), actions [performed] for the sake of maintaining the world [do not bind].
Or they do not bind the innate [karmas]. //41//
Madhusūdana:

In order to dispel such doubt, which is the root of all misfortune, the Lord speaks of the means for attaining certainty regarding the Self— the twofold steadfastness in Brahman consisting of action and knowledge, as described in the two preceding chapters according to the distinction between their earlier and later stages.
He explains this with two verses beginning with "yogena.
One who has renounced—that is, surrendered—actions to the Blessed Lord by means of *yoga*, which consists of the realization of equality characterized by the propitiation of the Blessed Lord;

or alternatively, one by whom actions have been renounced—that is, abandoned—by means of *yoga* characterized by the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Such a person is called "one who has renounced actions through yoga" (*yoga-saṃnyasta-karmāṇam*).

When doubt exists, how can there be the state of having actions renounced through yoga? To this he says: "one whose doubt is rent asunder by knowledge"—that is, one by whom doubt has been severed by means of knowledge characterized by certainty regarding the Self. Since the state of being subject to external objects is the very nature [of the mind], from what source does the arising of knowledge occur? To this he says: "the self-possessed," meaning one who is vigilant and always attentive. Such a person, possessing knowledge through vigilance and having his doubts rent asunder by knowledge—[is fit for yoga].

Actions—whether they be for the sake of maintaining the world or in the form of futile exertions—do not bind one whose actions have been renounced through Yoga; that is, O Dhanañjaya, they do not initiate a body characterized by undesirable, desirable, or mixed results.

Viśvanātha says: "But for such a person, there shall be freedom from action (naiṣkarmya)"; thus he speaks of one whose actions have been renounced immediately after the Yoga of desireless action (niṣkāma-karma-yoga), meaning one who has abandoned action through renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
And therefore, after the practice of knowledge, actions do not bind one who has severed doubt, who possesses self-control, and who has attained the inner Self. //41//
Baladeva: He says "by yoga" to show that for such a person there shall be perfection characterized by actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*).
[He refers to] one by whom actions have been renounced—that is, transformed into the form of knowledge—as stated in the passage "Established in yoga, perform actions";
and one whose doubts have been severed by the knowledge taught by Me.
Karmas do not bind one who possesses self-mastery and has beheld the Self, because of the disappearance of those [karmas] through knowledge. //42//
Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of knowledge this doubt of yours that has arisen from ignorance and resides in your heart, take refuge in yoga; arise, O Bharata! (42)
Śrīdhara: "Therefore" (tasmāt) means:

since this is so, therefore, having severed with the sword of the discrimination between the body and the Self this doubt—which has arisen from ignorance of the Self, resides in the heart, and is the cause of grief and other afflictions—take recourse to *karma-yoga*, which serves as the means for the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
And therein, first of all, rise for the battle that has been set forth; by addressing him as "O Bhārata," it is shown that war is a duty because of his status as a Kṣatriya. (42)
I bow to that Śauri, the cutter of all doubt, by whom the two-fold culmination— consisting of action and knowledge— was taught according to the distinctions of the stages of life and so forth.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Therefore, O Bhārata, having severed with the sword of knowledge this doubt of yours born of ignorance that dwells within the heart, take refuge in yoga and arise! 42.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Having cut through the doubt residing in the heart—that is, situated within the heart—resort to, or take refuge in, *yoga*, which is the yoga of action free from desire (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*).
"Arise to do battle"—this is the meaning. //42//
Among the means to liberation that have been mentioned, knowledge is praised here;
however, action alone is the means to that knowledge—thus has the meaning of this chapter been determined.
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, this fourth chapter has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 4.
Baladeva: "Therefore" means:

having cut asunder with the sword of knowledge taught by Me the doubt concerning the Self that resides within the heart—that is, has entered the heart—abide in the yoga of desireless action taught by Me; for that purpose, arise! //42//
Action consists of two parts, like grain from which the husk has been removed;
knowledge is superior by virtue of its substantial part—this is the conclusion regarding the Fourth State (turya). //4//
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad. //4//
